@article{smith2024corruption, ... }
@techreport{jones2024growth, ... }

% <<<SYNC-BIB:ZOTERO-END>>>

% <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-START>>>
% Hand-edited entries. Preserved across /sync-bib runs.

@unpublished{schmidt2024draft, ... }

% <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-END>>>

You have three ways to add a citation. Pick whichever fits how you work.

Default to Path 1. Use Path 2 only when you have full metadata in front of you and want the citation to resolve immediately (e.g., before a deadline). Use Path 3 only if you're already a Zotero user or want to invest the setup time.

docs.title: Path 1 — You just type the citation in .tex (citation-only)
docs.text:
Easiest. No setup needed.

  1. In your .tex file, write \citep{authorYEARkeyword} — e.g., \citep{jones2024corruption}.
  2. Don't touch references.bib.
  3. Record and share the change:
  4. Overleaf-mastered project: nothing more to do — Overleaf saves it.
  5. Git-mastered project, no terminal: open GitHub Desktop (free, https://desktop.github.com), which lists your changed .tex; type a one-line summary, click Commit, then Push origin. (Commit = record a snapshot; push = upload it so co-authors see it.)
  6. Terminal users: git add / git commit / git push per the handbook §2.3.

Whoever next runs /sync-bib will see your new citation surface as a "pending orphan" in project_management/zotero_todo.md. They'll source the paper into Zotero. Your \citep{...} will resolve in the next compile.

In the meantime, your compiled PDF will show [??] for the unresolved citation. That's expected — it'll resolve when the bib gets updated. Don't try to "fix" it yourself unless you're under a deadline (then use Path 2 below).

Before inventing a new citekey, search (Ctrl-F) references.bib AND project_management/zotero_todo.md for the first-author surname. Avoids the case where the paper is already pending under a slightly different key.

Disambiguation when Overleaf autocomplete suggests an existing key: pick a more specific keyword (gehring2025narrative already taken → use gehring2025refugees, gehring2025wartime, whatever the new paper is about). If you genuinely can't distinguish: letter suffix (smith2024a, smith2024b) is the fallback.

In long-form workflow doc, this is Workflow D.

docs.title: Path 2 — You write a bib entry by hand (manual bib edit)
docs.text:
For LaTeX-fluent people who'd rather add an entry directly:

  1. Open references.bib. Scroll to the MANUAL zone — do not edit the ZOTERO zone, those entries are auto-generated and your edits will be erased.
  2. Inside the MANUAL zone (between % <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-START>>> and % <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-END>>>), add your entry. Use the format described in principles/citation-style.md:
  3. @article for papers published in a journal
  4. @techreport for working papers (NBER, CEPR, IZA, SSRN, arXiv)
  5. @unpublished for circulated drafts / mimeo / unpublished manuscripts
  6. Before adding, search (Ctrl-F) the MANUAL zone for the first-author surname to avoid silent duplicates (the case where another co-author already added the same paper under a different citekey on a parallel branch).
  7. Get the core fields right (author, title, year, journal/institution + DOI if known). Style polish (Chicago title case, full author names, exact page-range format) gets normalized later by /fix-bib-in-zotero. Follow citation-style.md from the start if you can — it saves the bib_keeper time later.
  8. Commit and push.

Your entry survives indefinitely. Someone will eventually promote it to Zotero via /fix-bib-in-zotero. Until then, your bib entry is the source of truth.

In long-form workflow doc, this is Workflow E.

docs.title: Path 3 — You use Zotero
docs.text:
If you already have Zotero installed and use the browser Connector:

  1. In your browser, click the Zotero Connector button on the paper's page. Zotero saves the metadata + PDF.
  2. Ask whoever manages the Zotero library which group the project uses — they'll add you.
  3. After adding a few papers, run /sync-bib (if you have Claude Code) or wait for someone else to run it. New entries appear in the ZOTERO zone of references.bib.

If you want to run /sync-bib yourself, you'll need: - Zotero desktop running - Zotero Connector browser extension - Better BibTeX installed and configured (see install/install-better-bibtex.md) - Zotero MCP authenticated (see install/mcp-add-zotero.md)

This is optional. Path 1 or Path 2 work fine without any of this.

In long-form workflow doc, this is Workflow A.

docs.title: Choosing a citekey strategy (Path 3 users only)
docs.text:
Important constraint: Better BibTeX's citekey-generation formula is global per Zotero install — not per project, not per library. If you work on multiple papers with different citekey conventions (very common for active academics), you cannot satisfy all of them at once by changing the BBT formula.

The project's CLAUDE.md records a formula_mode to handle this:

Mode What it means Who picks this bib-canonical (recommended default) Treat the bib as source of truth. /sync-bib runs hygiene checks (orphans, collisions) but does NOT fetch new entries from BBT. To add a citation: hand-edit MANUAL zone of references.bib, or use a future /add-cite-from-zotero helper. Multi-project academics — the typical case formula-aligned Change your global BBT formula to match the project's. /sync-bib then fetches new entries from BBT and regenerates the ZOTERO zone. WARNING: affects every other project you cite from this Zotero install. Single-project users, or users whose projects all share one convention per-project-export Advanced. Configure BBT to auto-export a project-specific .bib with the project's formula. /sync-bib reads that file instead of querying BBT. Power users who set up per-project BBT auto-export

Check the project's CLAUDE.md zotero.formula_mode to see which mode is recorded. If you're not the bib_keeper, you don't need to change anything — just follow Path 1 (citation-only) or Path 2 (manual bib edit) and the bib_keeper handles the rest.

Switching modes mid-project: edit formula_mode in CLAUDE.md, commit, ask co-authors to do the same. Don't toggle frequently — pick a stable mode once and stick.

docs.title: The one convention worth keeping consistent
docs.text:
Citekey format: authorYEARkeyword — lowercase, no separators.

  • gehring2025narrative ✓
  • acemoglu2001colonial ✓
  • vanderberg2022growth ✓ (particles like "van der" join the surname; no spaces)
  • smith2024a / smith2024b ✓ (letter-suffix disambiguation as fallback)
  • Gehring_2025_Narrative ✗ (no underscores, no capitals)
  • Gehring2025 ✗ (missing keyword)

If you make up a citekey when adding a citation in Path 1, follow this format. The person who sources the paper into Zotero will use the same format, so your \citep{jones2024corruption} will resolve cleanly.

Year unknown at first citation? Use \cite{TODO_smith_corruption} — the TODO_ prefix tells /sync-bib to skip orphan detection for this key. Resolve later.

Special cases (single-name authors like Aristotle, institutional authors like World Bank, Asian names, Spanish double surnames, joint first authors): see citation-style.md §2.

Once a citekey appears in a shared PDF (referee version, JMP, working-paper distribution), it doesn't change. The bib_keeper sets draft_state: shared in CLAUDE.md when first sending the paper out — this mechanically protects all keys from being rewritten by /sync-bib.

docs.title: Habits that quietly break the bib for everyone
docs.text:
• Don't edit the ZOTERO zone of references.bib. It's regenerated on every /sync-bib. Edits are lost.
  • Don't delete the anchor tokens (% <<<SYNC-BIB:...-START>>> / -END>>>). They tell the script which zone is which. If they vanish, the script HALTs and points you at git history.
  • Don't open references.bib in any tool that auto-formats .bib files — JabRef, BibDesk, TeXstudio's .bib mode, VSCode with bibtex-tidy or LaTeX Workshop format-on-save enabled, vim/emacs with auto-format bibtex-mode hooks. They reorder or reformat entries and scramble the zones. Use a plain-text editor or Overleaf's editor.
  • Don't rename citekeys that have appeared in shared drafts. Once a paper has been circulated, its keys are frozen.
  • Don't hand-edit Zotero entries to fix typos in the rendered bib (Path 3 users). Run /fix-bib-in-zotero if you're the bib_keeper, or ask the bib_keeper to run it.

docs.title: Merge conflicts on references.bib
docs.text:
If git flags a conflict in references.bib, look at the markers:

  • Conflict in the ZOTERO zone — accept either side; the bib_keeper will re-run /sync-bib to regenerate. The ZOTERO zone is regenerated from Zotero, so the file content will resolve. If you don't have Claude Code, accept either side and commit.
  • Conflict in the MANUAL zone — both sets of new entries are real work; keep both. Don't blindly pick one side. Merge the entries manually: include all the @article{...} / @techreport{...} / @unpublished{...} blocks from both sides. If the conflict is intricate, /sync-bib --resolve-conflicts parses the markers and offers to merge both sides automatically.

docs.title: What to do when something goes wrong
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause What to do [??] in compiled PDF for a citation Orphan citekey — your .tex cites a key not yet in the bib Wait for next /sync-bib, or add the entry yourself via Path 2 (immediate resolution) Compile fails entirely (won't produce a PDF) BibTeX strict mode rejects undefined citations Path 2: add a real entry to MANUAL right now. Don't wait for the next sync. /sync-bib HALTs: "anchor tokens corrupted" A .bib formatter ate the markers git log -p references.bib → find last good version; revert or restore the markers manually. Then /sync-bib again. /sync-bib fails: "library X not accessible" You haven't been added to a declared Zotero group Ask whoever manages the Zotero group to add you in its group settings /sync-bib fails: "your BBT formula doesn't match the project's" Your Better BibTeX is generating different citekeys than the canonical ones Re-check install/install-better-bibtex.md formula; reinstall BBT with the pinned config Your .tex rename of a citekey doesn't take effect draft_state: shared flipped — keys are now frozen If paper has been shared, citekeys can't be rewritten silently — see "What NOT to do" Same paper appears twice in the rendered bib Two co-authors added it to MANUAL with different citekeys /sync-bib's DOI-collision check should catch this; if it didn't, surface to bib_keeper

docs.title: Per-project quirks
docs.text:
Read each project's CLAUDE.md once when you join. It's just a markdown file in the repo root — open it like any other doc. The zotero: block tells you: - Which Zotero libraries the project uses - Who the bib_keeper is — the one person authorized to run /fix-bib-in-zotero (the command that writes changes back to Zotero). Whoever the team designates. Anyone else can run /sync-bib (read-only) freely. - Whether the project is in drafting or shared state — controls whether /sync-bib rewrites your .tex keys (drafting) or renames Zotero entries (shared) on key mismatch.

If you're not the bib_keeper, don't run /fix-bib-in-zotero against the project — it writes to Zotero, and conflicts arise if two people run it on the same library. The bib_keeper field is also visible as a comment at the top of references.bib once /sync-bib has run.

docs.title: If you have Claude Code but no Zotero
docs.text: You can still run /sync-bib --read-only — it skips Zotero entirely and just runs orphan detection against your local bib, updating project_management/zotero_todo.md. Useful for seeing what's pending without needing Zotero auth. The flag auto-engages when no Zotero MCP is configured on your machine.

docs.title: Want more depth?
docs.text:
• principles/bibliography-and-literature.md — full workflow doc with rationale, all six workflows (A–F; this onboarding page is Workflow C), command list with phases.
  • principles/citation-style.md — what a bib entry should look like (entry types, title capitalization, author format, DOI, special citekey cases).
  • principles/academic-writing.md — broader writing guidance (paragraph structure, prose principles).
  • install/mcp-add-zotero.md — Zotero MCP setup (only if you want Path 3).
  • install/install-better-bibtex.md — Better BibTeX install (only if you want Path 3).

Most co-authors only need this doc. The references above are for the rare day-2 question.

docs.title: Co-author quickstart (start here)
docs.text:
For co-authors and RAs on a team already using this setup. Sizing it up for your own team instead? Start with why collaboration is hard.

This is the fast path: a one-time GitHub setup (~10 min, below), then day-to-day work by asking Claude Code in plain language — no terminal or git commands to memorize. You don't have to learn git to use it; you can pick up as much or as little as you like over time. Prefer to click or type yourself? The same workflow, entirely by hand, is in the handbook and the manual workflow. Everything here is the shortcut.

docs.title: The one idea that makes everything click
docs.text:
There is ONE repository, and it lives on GitHub. Your project folder on your laptop — and every clone_XX/ folder on a multi-author project — is just a local mirror of that one repository. They all sync to the same GitHub.

  • Dropbox keeps your mirror backed up and shares the heavy data files (which never go into git).
  • GitHub is where everyone's work actually meets.
  • Overleaf reads only GitHub's main branch.

Nobody "owns" the project. The top project folder is a shared container — it isn't a git repo at all; it just holds the data everyone shares and one personal clone per person (clone_XX/). You run git only inside your own clone, so two people can never collide on the same git. Everyone can push, and everyone can merge their own work. There is no gatekeeper, and no lead.

Hold onto that picture; every step below is just a consequence of it.

docs.title: What you do ONCE (the only real setup, ~10 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Install Claude Code — the desktop app from claude.com (or the CLI) — and sign in with your Claude subscription.
  2. Get GitHub access, once. Accept the repository invitation (it arrives by email). Then open Claude Code in any folder and say:

    "Help me sign in to GitHub so I can push and pull." Claude walks you through it (usually: install GitHub Desktop, sign in once — that quietly handles authentication forever). You do this one time per computer.

  3. Tell Claude who you are, once — so your name is stamped on your work:

    "Set my git name to 'Your Name' and email to you@university.edu."

That's the entire setup. You never repeat it on this machine.

docs.title: Then: everything is a sentence to Claude Code
docs.text:
Open Claude Code inside your project folder — the one Dropbox already synced to C:\Users\<you>\Dropbox\<project>\. (To do that: in the Claude Code desktop app use Open folder and pick it; or, in the terminal, cd into the folder and run claude. Your project arrived via Dropbox — you do not download it from GitHub.)

Multi-clone projects: if your project folder contains clone_<XX>/ sub-folders (or its CLAUDE.md has a "Multi-clone layout" block), open Claude Code in your own clone_<XX>/ instead of the top folder — everywhere below, "your project folder" means your clone. Not sure which kind you're on? Ask a co-author, or see why. Single-clone projects: the top folder is correct, read on. Claude reads the project's rules on the way in, so it knows the safety conventions. Then just say what you want — in plain words; you don't need the exact phrasing below:

You want to… Say to Claude Code… What actually happens Get set up to work here "Help me set up my own copy to work on this project." Claude walks you through the short one-time setup of your personal copy (or tells you it's already set up). A few steps, once. Save your work "Commit my work." Claude records a snapshot of your changes, with a short note. Share it / back it up "Push my branch to GitHub." Your snapshots go up to GitHub — your off-machine backup, and how the team can get your work. Touches nothing in the shared paper. Propose it for the paper "Open a pull request for my work." Claude opens a pull request on GitHub — a tidy "here's what I changed, please pull it in." Actually put it in the paper (on GitHub, click Merge — or "merge my pull request") Merging the PR into main is the step that reaches the paper. This is a GitHub action, not something Claude does silently — see "two things" below. Get the team's latest "Bring in the latest changes from the team." Claude pulls everyone's merged work into your copy. Check you're working safely "Am I in the right folder to run git here?" Claude runs a quick check and tells you.

Why this path is recommended: when the project is set up for it (its CLAUDE.md carries the team conventions), Claude reads those rules and keeps you on the rails — it won't run git in the shared container folder, won't stage data or secrets, and checks you're in your own copy first. Raw git by hand has none of that. It's not magic, though: if something looks off, Claude tells you and you decide — so the conversational path is easier and safer, not hands-off.

Everything above you can also do by hand — Claude just saves the typing and remembers the rules. Here's the core save-and-share loop both ways:

Ask Claude CodeBy hand

"Commit my work, push my branch, and open a pull request."

Claude stages your changed files (explicit paths, never git add -A), commits with a sensible message, pushes, and opens the PR — pausing for your OK before the push.

git add <file>                 # explicit paths, never `git add -A`
git commit -m "what changed"
git push                       # then open the PR on GitHub

The full by-hand reference is the manual workflow.

docs.title: Two things every co-author gets wrong (now you won't)
docs.text:
1. Pushing is not the same as putting it in the paper. The full chain is:

    your branch → push to GitHub → merge into main → Overleaf "pull from GitHub"

Until the merge into main step, the paper (and Overleaf, if the paper uses it) don't see your work. So "I pushed it" is not "it's in the paper" — the merge is the missing link. (On an Overleaf-mastered project the paper text lives in Overleaf, not the repo, so this chain applies to your code and figures, not the .tex — ask a co-author if unsure.)

  1. You're allowed to merge your own work — but check what your team expects. On a standard private repo GitHub doesn't force a reviewer, so technically you can merge your own pull request. Whether you should is a team norm: a co-author often just merges; a research assistant usually wants the PI to look first. When in doubt, open the PR and say "ask a co-author to review" rather than self-merging. "Allowed" and "expected" are different things — this guide tells you what's allowed; your team tells you what's expected.

docs.title: If you use Codex instead of Claude Code
docs.text: Codex does not automatically read the project's rules, so the safety guardrails don't apply on their own. Two options: prefer Claude Code for anything touching git, or — if you stay in Codex — open the project's CLAUDE.md, read its "Multi-clone layout" section yourself, and be deliberate. The one rule that matters most: never run git in the project root (the top folder); only in your own clone_XX/.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• The daily rhythm, editing the paper text, and the full "when something breaks" playbook → co-author handbook.
  • Confused by a word (clone, branch, push, merge, pull request)? → plain-language primer.
  • Want the AI writing/review tools too (drafting, referee reports, figures)? → what the toolkit is — optional, not needed for the above.

docs.title: Something broke — fixes & recovery
docs.text: Why this page exists. Almost every problem a newcomer hits on this setup is one of a small, known set — and each has a calm, specific fix. This is the page to skim before you panic and the page to search when something looks broken. Most of these are not real damage; they're the structure doing its job in a way that's unfamiliar. Nothing here requires you to be a git expert. When in doubt, the safest move is almost always "stop and ask a co-author" — listed where it applies.

docs.title: Setup and environment
docs.text:
"Rscript / python is not recognized." The program is installed but not on your PATH (the default on Windows). Use the full path from the project's CLAUDE.md instead of the bare name — e.g. "C:\Program Files\R\R-4.4.3\bin\Rscript.exe" code/00_setup.R. If it's genuinely not installed, install R from cran.r-project.org (plain R, you don't need RStudio for setup).

Dropbox folder looks empty or half-there. Wait for the Dropbox tray icon to show a green tick — that means everything has actually downloaded. A folder that's still syncing looks like missing files but isn't. Don't start work (or git operations) until it's green.

"My clone has data/ and literature/ folders too — is that duplication?" No. Inside a clone those folders hold only the tracked skeletons (codebooks, .bib) — a few MB. The heavy raw data and PDFs are gitignored and live once in the shared container. Don't "clean up" the skeletons; they're meant to be there.

Scripts can't find the data. Your clone reaches the shared data through a .data-in-parent marker file at the clone root. If it's missing, create it (touch .data-in-parent) and re-run code/00_setup.*. The setup script's banner should show the data paths pointing at ../data/.

docs.title: "Where did my work go?"
docs.text:
A "conflicted copy" file appeared. Two people (or your own two machines) wrote the same file and Dropbox kept both. Don't delete either blindly — open both, reconcile by hand, keep the right content, then delete the "conflicted copy". Prevent it by the golden rule: one writer per file.

"My file is in Dropbox but a co-author says it's not in git." Both can be true — Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence. A file is only in the project's real history once you git add + commit + push it. Hand-copying into Dropbox is not enough; commit it too.

"I think I lost work." Usually you didn't. Unpushed commits still live in your clone (and Dropbox backs the clone up). Check git status and git log in your clone first; the work is very often right there. If still stuck, ask a co-author before doing anything destructive.

docs.title: git and clones
docs.text:
Claude opened in the wrong folder / "am I in the right place?" Run the clone-discipline check (or ask Claude "check clone discipline"). It tells you whether you're inside your clone (good) or at the shared container (move into your clone). In the leaderless model there's no "lead" to worry about — the check is purely "are you in a clone?".

"git push was rejected." Someone else's work landed on the branch first. Pull it in, then push: git fetch origin && git merge origin/main, resolve any conflicts, git push. This is normal, not an error.

"git pull says up to date but main has clearly moved on." Your clone is pinned to your own branch, so a plain pull only fetches your branch. Bring main in explicitly: git fetch origin && git merge origin/main. Do this every few days and always before opening a pull request.

"There's a .git at the shared container root." That's a legacy layout from before the leaderless migration, and it's the one genuinely risky state — a shared root repo whose branch can flip under everyone. Don't run git at the root. Work in your clone, and flag it so the project gets migrated (see the canonical spec, "Multi-clone pattern").

docs.title: Overleaf
docs.text:
A figure I fixed in Overleaf reverted. Figures travel code → git → Overleaf, one way. Editing a figure inside Overleaf gets overwritten on the next regeneration. Fix the script that makes the figure, commit, then bring it into Overleaf. (See the manual workflow.)

"Who can change the Overleaf project?" One person coordinates the Overleaf sync (the Overleaf admin role) so two people don't push conflicting versions through the bridge. That's a one-job designation, not a hierarchy — everyone is still an equal co-author.

docs.title: "We've been copying .tex from Overleaf by hand"
docs.text:
A common habit worth correcting: someone writes in Overleaf, then copies the .tex (or a PDF) into the Dropbox folder by hand. It looks fine — Dropbox and Overleaf match — but git silently falls behind (Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence), and you end up with two diverging copies of a file that git is supposed to own.

The fix, easiest first:

  • Best — sync through git, don't copy. Use Overleaf's own git access to push/pull between Overleaf and git. Then git is always current and there's nothing to hand-copy; Dropbox updates itself via your clone.
  • If a file did get hand-copied (it happens), the one-line rescue is to also commit and push it to git right after — so the canonical history stops trailing what everyone is reading.
  • Stop hand-copying anything that lives in git. Edit it through git and let it flow; copying tracked files by hand is what creates the diverging copies in the first place.

(The standard flow this replaces is in the manual workflow.)

docs.title: When in doubt
docs.text: Some failure modes — especially multi-clone confusion — are hard to diagnose from a description. Ask a co-author; it's faster and safer than guessing, and it's never the wrong call.

docs.title: Why git, Dropbox, Overleaf & LaTeX
docs.text: Why the toolkit is built the way it is. Nothing here is needed to use it — but understanding the why makes the rules stick, and tells you when a rule does NOT apply. ~5 minutes. For term definitions, see the primer.

docs.title: 1. The two-layer model: Dropbox carries files, GitHub carries meaning
docs.text:
Each layer fails alone. Dropbox can't tell you which version of the code produced the figure in the submitted paper, can't host a review step, and silently lets two editors overwrite each other. Git chokes on gigabytes of data and has no instant sync. Together, each covers the other's gap:

flowchart TB
    subgraph DB["Dropbox — the storage layer"]
        D1["data/ — THE single copy<br/>(gitignored, never duplicated)"]
        D2["instant sync + backup<br/>of everything, incl. unpushed work"]
    end
    subgraph GH["GitHub — the meaning layer"]
        G1["commits: who changed what, when"]
        G2["branches + PRs: review before<br/>anything becomes 'production'"]
        G3["main: always compiles,<br/>always reproducible"]
    end
    DB ---|"same folder,<br/>two record-keepers"| GH

Every hard rule in the handbook is a consequence: data never goes in git (layer 1 owns it), work reaches the team only via push + PR (layer 2 owns meaning), and saving a file shares nothing (saving talks to layer 1 only).

docs.title: 2. One canonical file per artefact
docs.text: No paper_v2.tex, no 02_analysis_final.R. One file; git carries the history. Reasons: (a) filename versions force every reader to guess which is current — git's history doesn't; (b) "v2" conflates document type with revision (a real paper_v1.tex once turned out to be a conference abstract); (c) scripts and tools can rely on stable paths. When you want to experiment freely: that's what a branch is — a whole-project "v2" that can't disturb anyone and gets reviewed before merging.

docs.title: 3. Branch isolation, end to end
docs.text:
The thing that goes wrong in shared folders is uncoordinated parallel work. The system isolates parallel work at three levels:

flowchart LR
    subgraph You["your branch / your clone"]
        A["edit code + paper"] --> B["outputs land in<br/>output/_exploratory/<branch>/"]
        B --> C["copy final exhibit to<br/>output/figures/ (tracked)"]
    end
    C --> D["push + PR"]
    D --> E["review"]
    E --> F["merge to main:<br/>script + exhibit + text<br/>arrive together"]
  • Code and text: your branch — invisible to main until merged.
  • Exhibits: the setup scripts auto-redirect outputs to output/_exploratory/<branch>/ so two people's figures never overwrite. Promotion to the canonical output/figures/ is YOUR explicit copy on the branch — the PR then carries script, exhibit and paper text as one reviewable package. (Nothing moves "automatically on merge"; git merges files, it doesn't run pipelines.)
  • On multi-clone projects, whole working copies: each co-author has their own nested clone (clone_XX/) pinned to their branch, so even Dropbox-level sync can't mix two people's work-in-progress. Only the data stays shared — one copy, reached via a marker file.

docs.title: 4. Replication-first structure
docs.text: The folder layout (data/raw read-only, data/processed regenerable, numbered scripts, flat output/) mirrors what the AEA Data Editor expects in a replication package. The payoff: when the paper is accepted, the replication archive is a packaging step, not a re-engineering project. The same logic drives the data/raw/ read-only hard rule — every result must be reproducible from raw by re-running the pipeline, which is impossible if raw was ever edited in place.

docs.title: 5. Drift resistance: documents lie, generators don't
docs.text: This repo's measured failure mode is documentation going stale (~2-week half-life on inventory docs). The countermeasures are structural, not aspirational: the INDEX is generated from the tools' own metadata and a release check fails if it drifts; the recipes page is grep-checked against the actual command files; canonical specs that ship mirror copies are diff-checked; and the setup templates have a 19-check regression harness. Rule of thumb the team learned the hard way: a claim that something "works" counts only after it has been executed.

docs.title: 6. Why the AI layer is safe to let loose
docs.text: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md (project rules) plus the user-level rules on every session start. The riskiest operations are gated regardless of what you ask for: pushes need explicit confirmation, data/raw/ writes are refused, broad staging (git add .) is blocked, destructive git operations require approval. That's why the handbook can honestly tell a novice that almost nothing here is unrecoverable if you stop and ask before improvising: the guardrails are in the tool's standing orders, not in the user's discipline.

docs.title: 7. The writing layer: LaTeX and Overleaf
docs.text: The two layers above explain why the project is structured this way; the paper itself rests on one more choice — LaTeX. Plain-text source is what makes the rest work: git can diff it line by line, Claude can edit it directly, and the output is reproducible. Overleaf is an optional add-on for browser compiling and track-changes review of prose (a paid feature the project owner sets up); you can compile LaTeX locally without it. The how-to for both is in LaTeX and Overleaf.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Short answers to the questions that come up most. Each links to the page with the full story.

Is this the only "right" way to do things? No. It's a working solution. The genuinely required rules are short (never overwrite raw data; commit-to-share; one writer per file; exhibits trace to code); everything else — the exact layout, Dropbox, Overleaf, the tools — is a recommendation you can adapt. → required vs. recommended

Do I need to know git? No — you can pick it up gradually. Claude Code (or GitHub Desktop) handles the mechanics, and the primer defines every term in plain language.

Do I need Claude Code / an AI tool at all? No. Everything works by hand — Claude is a convenience, never a dependency. → the manual workflow, choosing your setup

Do I need Dropbox? Do I need Overleaf? Dropbox is the recommended default (backup + sharing), but a pure-GitHub setup works too. Overleaf is usually not needed — everything compiles locally; its one real draw is track-changes review of prose. → choosing your setup, new to Overleaf?

Who's the lead / who's in charge? Nobody — it's leaderless. Every co-author is equal; main lives on GitHub, owned by no one; anyone can push and merge. → why collaboration is hard

Where's the latest paper? Which clone has it? The canonical version is main on GitHub. On team projects, the shared container also keeps a read-only copy of the current paper so you never have to hunt through clones. → what goes where

What if I mess up or lose work? Almost nothing here is unrecoverable if you stop and ask before improvising — git history and Dropbox both back you up. → common issues

How do I actually run a skill? Three ways: a slash command (/name), just describe the task in plain language, or let it auto-trigger (a nudge, not a guarantee). → how skills are triggered

How do I set up a new — or existing — project? New: /bootstrap-project. Existing/messy: back up first, then /refactor-structure. → what goes where → "turning a messy project into this"

How do I update the toolkit later? /plugin marketplace update kai-team-claude + restart Claude Code; re-run the install script for the ~/.claude skills. → install the toolkit, updates

Is my data safe? data/raw/ is read-only — never overwritten; data/processed/ is rebuildable from raw + code. There's even a guard that asks before any code writes to raw. → working with the shared data

Where do I read these docs / is this online? Yes — the hosted site is at kaligi.github.io/kai-team-claude-docs (search + sidebar; nothing to install, just open the link). The editable source lives in the private GitHub repo under docs/ (ask Kai for an invite). The website is auto-published from there into a separate public repo that contains only the built HTML — so the page is public even though the toolkit's source isn't. You read on the website; you install the toolkit from the private repo (Install).

docs.title: Quick wins to try first
docs.text:
Why start here. The fastest way to trust a new tool is to get one real, useful result out of it in five minutes — before committing to any workflow. Each thing below is self-contained: it works on its own, doesn't touch the collaboration setup, doesn't need you to learn git, and gives you something you'd actually want. Pick one, try it on a real paper of yours, and see whether it earns its place.

A note on honesty: these run on Claude Code with your own Claude subscription, and the data-figure one fetches from public data sources over the internet. They are genuinely useful, not magic — Claude can be wrong, so read its output the way you'd read a sharp RA's first draft.

docs.title: 1. A hostile pre-submission review — adversarial-review
docs.text:
The most valuable thing an AI can do for a paper is attack it. Ask:

"Run an adversarial review of this introduction." (paste it, or give a path)

The reviewer is explicitly tasked to find flaws — weak identification claims, overclaiming, gaps a referee would pounce on — not to reassure you. It's deliberately not balanced unless you ask for balance. Use it on a section you think is finished; it usually isn't.

docs.title: 2. A writing-quality diagnosis — scientific-writing-analysis
docs.text:
For prose rather than argument, this runs a structured analysis based on Lebrun's Scientific Writing — paragraph progression, lead sentences, topic-stress flow. Ask:

"Analyze the writing quality of this section."

You get specific, located feedback ("the lead of paragraph 7 doesn't connect to paragraph 6"), not vague "tighten this up" notes.

docs.title: 3. A publication-quality figure from real data — real-data-figure
docs.text:
Want a clean figure of, say, GDP per capita or battle deaths over time, without hunting down the data yourself? Ask:

"Make a time-series figure of for from World Bank data."

It sources from OWID / World Bank / V-Dem and others, and produces a publication-quality plot. This one needs internet access (it's fetching real data) and an R/Python environment — the most "setup-ish" of the four, but also the most impressive when it lands.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: If one of these earned its keep and you want to use Claude on a shared project with co-authors, that's where the collaboration setup comes in — start with why collaboration is hard, then the quickstart. If you'd rather understand what Claude Code actually is first, read how Claude Code thinks.

docs.title: How Claude Code thinks (so you know what to expect)
docs.text: Why this matters. Most frustration with AI tools comes from a wrong mental model — expecting magic and getting a literal-minded assistant, or expecting a chatbot and getting something that can actually change your files. This page gives you an accurate picture of what Claude Code is, so your expectations match reality. No overpromising: knowing the limits is what lets you use it well.

docs.title: What it actually is
docs.text:
Claude Code is an assistant that runs in a folder on your computer and can do three concrete things, with your permission:

  1. Read the files in that folder (and ones you point it at).
  2. Run commands — git, R, Python, LaTeX — the same ones you'd type yourself.
  3. Edit files — make the change, not just describe it.

That's the whole superpower: it's not a chat window that gives advice, it's something that can do the work in your project. Everything else follows from those three.

docs.title: Chat vs. a "harness" — the distinction that trips people up
docs.text:
If the only AI you've used is a chat window (claude.ai, ChatGPT), the key shift is this: a chat can only talk back. You paste text in, you get text out; it never touches your computer. Claude Code is a harness — software that wraps the same underlying model and gives it hands: it can open your files, edit them, and run commands, right where your project lives.

Chat (claude.ai) A harness (Claude Code, Codex) Sees your files no — only what you paste yes — the folder you open it in Changes files / runs code no yes, with your approval Good for quick questions, drafting in the window doing the actual work in your repo

The word "harness" is borrowed from the idea of a harness on a working animal: it doesn't make the model smarter, it lets it pull the cart — act on your machine instead of just describing what to do. The trade for that power is the permission step: because it can act, it asks before anything consequential (next section). It is not autopilot.

docs.title: The three things to internalize
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    F["The folder you open it in<br/>= its whole world"]
    P["It asks permission<br/>before changing things"]
    M["No memory between sessions<br/>unless it's written down"]

1. It acts on the folder you open it in. This is the single most important fact. Claude Code's "world" is the folder you start it in. Open it in your clone_<XX>/ (your personal copy of a shared project — explained in Working together; ignore the term for now if you're working solo) and your work lands there; open it at the shared container and it would touch shared files. This is why the collaboration setup insists you open it in your own clone — it's not bureaucracy, it's how the tool is wired. (See why collaboration is hard.)

2. It asks before doing anything consequential. Editing files, running commands, pushing to git — you approve these. You're never one typo away from disaster; there's a checkpoint. You can tell it to stop at any point, and local changes are easy to roll back (git keeps your history). The one thing that isn't a free undo is something already pushed and merged to the shared main — that's why pushes ask first. Treat the approval prompts as a feature, not friction: glance at what it's about to do.

3. It has no memory between sessions — unless it's written down. Close the session and it forgets everything. What persists is what lives in files: most importantly a CLAUDE.md in the project, which it reads at the start of every session. That's how a project teaches Claude its conventions ("we use R and tidyverse", "this paper is Overleaf-mastered", "never edit raw data"). If you want it to remember something, the answer is usually "put it in CLAUDE.md", not "tell it again".

docs.title: What it's good at, and where to be careful
docs.text:
Good at Be careful with Boilerplate, refactors, "do this 40 times" Anything it can't verify — it can state a wrong fact confidently Remembering rules so you don't have to Numbers and citations — check them like a referee would Driving git/LaTeX/R you'd have to look up Big irreversible actions — read the diff before approving First drafts you then sharpen Treating its output as final — it's a strong first pass, not a verdict

The honest summary: it's like a fast, tireless, occasionally overconfident RA. It will save you real time, and it will sometimes be wrong in a way that sounds right. The workflow around it — approvals, git history, reading the diff — exists precisely so that "sometimes wrong" is cheap to catch and undo.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Try it on something real: first things to try
  • Use it on a shared project: co-author quickstart
  • Prefer to drive everything yourself: the manual workflow

docs.title: How it works — skills, processes & gates
docs.text:
People keep asking the same fair question: when the toolkit "does a process" — like iterating over a figure before showing it to me — what is that, actually? Is it a program running in the background? Where does it live on my computer? Once you see how a "process" is built, you can read it, change it, and add your own.

The short version: everything here is just files on disk — readable text, plus a few small scripts. Nothing runs in the background. A "process" is either a set of instructions Claude follows when you ask, or a script that fires automatically on an event.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
Six things, and they're all plain files you can open:

  • Skill — a folder with a SKILL.md (Markdown instructions) plus, optionally, bundled scripts/ (Python/R) and reference docs. Triggering a skill means Claude reads the instructions and follows them — running any bundled script along the way.
  • Command — a skill you invoke by name with a leading slash (/review-paper). It's the same thing as a skill, just with an explicit handle.
  • Agent — a Markdown spec describing a focused sub-worker (e.g. a bibliography auditor). A skill can dispatch several agents to work in parallel.
  • Plugin — a bundle of related commands + skills + agents (e.g. academic-workflow). Installing one gives you everything inside it.
  • Principle — a shared rules file (the writing, citation, and git conventions in principles/). Skills and agents read these, so fixing a rule once propagates everywhere.
  • Hook — an actual executable script wired into settings.json that runs automatically and deterministically on a tool event (for example, the raw-data guard runs before any write to data/raw/ and asks first).

How they fit together:

flowchart TD
    MP["Marketplace<br/>(this repo's catalogue)"] --> PL
    subgraph PL["Plugin — e.g. academic-workflow"]
        CMD["Commands<br/>/review-paper"]
        SK["Skills<br/>kai-writing"]
        AG["Agents<br/>bibliography-auditor"]
    end
    CMD -->|"named handle for"| SK
    SK -->|"dispatches"| AG
    PR["Principles<br/>writing · citations · git rules"]
    SK -.->|"reads"| PR
    AG -.->|"reads"| PR
    HK["Hook<br/>guard_raw_data.py"] ==>|"fires on a tool event<br/>(deterministic)"| EV["before a write to data/raw/"]

docs.title: Two ways a process is enforced — and the difference matters
docs.text:
There are two levels of enforcement:

How it's encoded Guarantee Soft (a rule) instructions in a skill's Markdown Claude usually does it — it's an instruction the model follows, not a law Hard (a gate / hook) an actual script that runs no matter what deterministic — runs every time its event fires

Most of the toolkit is soft: a skill says "do it properly" and Claude follows. That's flexible and covers the vast majority of work. A hard gate (a hook, or a deterministic check script) is what you reach for when "usually" isn't good enough — safety rails (never overwrite raw data) or a step you want guaranteed to run.

You can promote a soft rule to a hard gate when it earns it: take an instruction the model sometimes skips, and wire it as a hook so it always fires. This is how the toolkit hardens over time.

docs.title: A worked example: iterating over a figure before you see it
docs.text:
You ask for a figure. Behind the scenes the figure skill's instructions say: build it → render it → look for the obvious problems (a legend overlapping a bar, unreadable labels, a wrong unit) → fix them → repeat once or twice → then show you. So what reaches you is a checked draft, not a raw first attempt, and you don't waste time flagging mistakes the agent could see itself.

Today that loop is soft — it lives as instructions in the figure skill, and Claude follows them when you invoke it. To make it hard (guaranteed, and automatic for any figure, not just ones made via the skill), you'd add a hook that fires after a figure file is written and runs the check itself. That upgrade — auto-firing the self-check — is on the roadmap; see Self-correcting figures for the patterns you can use today (including a global instruction that turns the self-check on everywhere).

docs.title: Where it all lives on your computer
docs.text:
Plain files, all version-controlled in the repo and copied to your machine by the install script — nothing is a compiled black box:

  • ~/.claude/skills/<name>/ — skills (SKILL.md + any scripts)
  • ~/.claude/agents/ — agent specs
  • ~/.claude/principles/ — the shared rules
  • plugins — managed by Claude Code's own registry (the slash-commands)
  • settings.json — where hooks are wired to events

You can open any of them, read exactly what they do, and edit them. That's the point: the "processes" aren't magic — they're instructions and small scripts you own.

docs.text: → What the toolkit is for the catalogue view, or Working with Claude Code for the day-to-day patterns (permission modes, plan-then-check, self-correcting figures).

docs.title: How merging works (and when to coordinate)
docs.text: Collaborating on code and text comes down to one question: when can two people work at once, and when do they have to take turns? The answer is in how git merges. This page builds it up from the bottom.

docs.title: Git's unit is the line
docs.text:
Git stores text as lines and merges line by line. It does not understand meaning — it only asks: did you two change the same lines, or different lines?

This has a practical consequence you've probably felt:

  • In code (R, Python, Stata) you naturally write one statement per line, so git's line-unit lines up with logical units. Two people editing different statements are editing different lines, and git merges them cleanly.
  • In LaTeX a whole paragraph is often one long line, so two people editing the same paragraph are editing the same line — git sees a clash even if they changed different sentences. The fix is a real best practice: write .tex with one sentence per line (semantic line breaks). Then git's line-unit works for prose too, and a clash shrinks to the actual sentence in dispute instead of the whole paragraph.

docs.title: Three things that happen when two people's work meets
1. Clean merge — different lines — safe and automatic
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Anc["common version"] --> A["Ann edits line 3"]
    Anc --> B["Ben edits line 9"]
    A --> M["git keeps BOTH"]
    B --> M
    M --> R["line 3 = Ann's,<br/>line 9 = Ben's<br/>no conflict"]

Different lines (or different files) → git takes both, automatically. You edit the abstract, your coauthor edits the appendix → both land, even straight on main.

docs.title: 2. Textual conflict — same line — git stops you (safe)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Anc["line 3: original"] --> A["Ann: line 3 = version A"]
    Anc --> B["Ben: line 3 = version B"]
    A --> C{"same line,<br/>two versions"}
    B --> C
    C --> H["git STOPS and marks a conflict;<br/>a human picks. Annoying, never lost."]

The same line changed two ways → git refuses to guess, marks a conflict, and a human chooses. This is the safe kind: git won't let it slip past you.

docs.title: 3. Logical conflict — different lines, but broken — git stays SILENT (the danger)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Anc["code uses variable: income"] --> A["Ann (line 10):<br/>rename income to inc"]
    Anc --> B["Ben (line 80):<br/>new code uses income"]
    A --> M["different lines →<br/>git merges cleanly,<br/>NO conflict flagged"]
    B --> M
    M --> X["line 80 now breaks:<br/>income no longer exists.<br/>git never warned you."]

Different lines, but one change breaks the other's assumptions → git merges with no warning, and the result is broken. Git reads lines, not meaning. This is the one to watch for — the conflicts git shouts about are the safe ones; the silent break is the dangerous one.

docs.title: "Both add something after line 150 — whose goes first?"
docs.text:
Two cases, and the difference matters:

  • Different actual lines (Ann adds after line 150, Ben after line 160) → git keeps both, in file order — line 150's addition, then line 160's. No conflict.
  • The same spot (both add right after line 150) → git does not pick an order. It raises an "add/add" conflict at that point, shows both, and a human decides the order (or keeps both).
flowchart LR
    Anc["line 150"] --> A["Ann adds X right after 150"]
    Anc --> B["Ben adds Y right after 150"]
    A --> M{"same insertion point"}
    B --> M
    M --> H["add/add CONFLICT —<br/>a human chooses the order.<br/>git will not decide."]

Important: the order you merge in does not auto-decide the result. Merging Ann-then-Ben vs Ben-then-Ann doesn't make one "win" — git still surfaces the clash and whoever resolves it chooses. In the pull-request flow this is tidy: the first PR merges cleanly; the second PR is now behind main, so its author pulls main, hits the add/add conflict, and picks the order before merging.

docs.title: So when can you work in parallel?
docs.text:
Situation What git does What you do Both ADD independent things (a new analysis block, a new figure script in a new file, different paper sections) merges cleanly, and it works work in parallel — nothing special Both edit the SAME lines (same paragraph, same function) conflict — git stops you resolve by hand, or agree who does it. Annoying, not dangerous One changes a SHARED FOUNDATION (data cleaning, variable definitions, the early analysis others build on) often merges silently, then breaks downstream coordinate: one person at a time, announce it, everyone re-pulls and re-runs after. git will not protect you here

The pattern: independent additions are the safe parallel case; shared-foundation changes must be serial and announced — because that's exactly the silent, logical break git can't catch.

docs.title: Branches and pull requests: where a human catches what git can't
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    BR["your branch<br/>(work in isolation)"] --> PR["pull request"]
    PR --> RV["review:<br/>a human reads the meaning"]
    RV --> MG["merge to main"]

Branches keep each person's half-finished work off main. The review step is where a person catches the logical conflict git can't see — "wait, you renamed the variable my new code uses." Git merges the text; the review merges the meaning. That is the real reason the workflow routes everything through a PR instead of letting everyone push straight to main.

docs.title: Resolving a conflict, step by step
docs.text:
First figure out which kind you have — they live in different systems and you fix them in different places:

  • A git conflict — on your tracked files (code, paper) when you pull main into your branch and the same lines were changed two ways. You fix it in your own clone, locally (not on GitHub).
  • A Dropbox "conflicted copy" — only on the shared container files that live in Dropbox and are not in anyone's git clone (data/processed/, literature/, project_management/). Two people edited the same shared file at once, so Dropbox kept both and renamed one. You fix it in Dropbox.
  • The silent logical break (different lines, one breaks the other) is not flagged by either system — a person catches it. Covered last.

docs.title: A git conflict
docs.text:
You see it after git merge origin/main (or when opening a PR): git prints CONFLICT and lists the files.

With Claude Code (recommended)By hand

Say: "I have a merge conflict — show me each one, explain both sides, and propose a resolution." Claude reads the markers, tells you what each side changed and why, proposes the merged text, and (once you approve) stages and commits. You never touch the marker syntax. If you want to bail out: "abort the merge" puts you back where you started.

  1. git status — lists the conflicted files.
  2. Open one. The clash is wrapped in markers: 
    <<<<<<< HEAD          (your branch)
your version
=======
the incoming version (from main)
>>>>>>> origin/main
  3. Edit that region to what you want — keep yours, keep theirs, or combine — and delete all three marker lines.
  4. git add <file> to mark it resolved. Repeat for each file.
  5. git commit (finishes the merge), then git push.
  6. Wrong turn? git merge --abort returns you exactly to the start — nothing lost.

Either way it happens in your clone, locally — that's where the files and the merge live. GitHub's web editor can handle a trivial one-file conflict, but local is the normal path, and Claude Code makes it painless. So no: a git conflict is not something you can only fix "on GitHub."

docs.title: A Dropbox conflicted copy
docs.text:
Dropbox leaves a second file next to the original, named like TODO (Ann's conflicted copy 2026-06-16).md. Nothing is lost — both versions are sitting there.

With Claude CodeBy hand

Say: "Dropbox made a conflicted copy of <file> — diff it against the original, merge the two into one, then delete the copy." Claude shows the differences, merges them, and removes the stray file.

  1. Open the original and the "(conflicted copy)" file side by side.
  2. Copy any edits that exist only in the conflicted copy into the original.
  3. Save the original and delete the conflicted-copy file.
  4. Unsure what changed? Dropbox's Version history on the original shows the timeline.

This only ever happens on the shared container files. To prevent it: give each shared file an owner, edit it one person at a time, or — for anything that benefits from history — keep it in git instead of the plain container.

docs.title: The silent logical break
docs.text: Neither git nor Dropbox flags this one (different lines, but one change breaks the other's assumptions). A person catches it — usually at PR review, or when a script suddenly errors. The fix isn't mechanical: re-pull, re-run, and talk to whoever changed the shared foundation so you both build on the new version. That's exactly why foundational changes are coordinated up front rather than merged blindly.

docs.text: → Why collaboration is hard · Daily workflow (handbook)

docs.title: Install the Claude Code toolkit
docs.text:
Why bother. This is what turns Claude Code from a generic assistant into one that knows economics-paper conventions — drafting in your voice, referee reports, figures from real data, citation hygiene. If that payoff isn't worth a one-time setup to you yet, skip it; the collaboration workflow works without it. (New to what "skills", "plugins", and "the marketplace" mean? Read what the toolkit is first — two minutes.)

This is the optional toolkit install: Claude Code + the Zotero bridge + the plugin marketplace, so you get the writing helpers, review pipelines, and figure tools. If you only want to work on a shared paper (git + your stats software), you do not need this — see the co-author quickstart instead.

Assumes no command-line experience: every step is copy-paste. Stuck? Ask whoever set you up, or open an issue on the repo, with the exact error text + the step number.

docs.title: What you'll have when you're done
docs.text:
Once setup is finished, in any terminal you can type claude to start a Claude Code session. Inside that session you can:

  • Type /academic to launch a multi-agent review of a paper or chapter
  • Type /review-paper to get a 6-agent referee report on a draft
  • Type /review-paper-light for a fast 2-agent contribution-and-identification check
  • Type /bootstrap-project on day 1 of a new project to scaffold a CLAUDE.md and working/ folder
  • Ask Claude to "draft this paragraph in Kai's style" → the kai-writing skill kicks in
  • Ask Claude to search Zotero for a paper, fetch the BibTeX, and add it to the project's bib file
  • Ask Claude to draft a TikZ diagram, build a real-data figure, or design a seminar talk
  • Ask Claude to help turn open-ended survey answers into validated variables → the qualitative-survey-coding skill kicks in

You'll also have access to the project's shared folders (Dropbox, GitHub, Overleaf, Zotero group library) once those per-project invitations are sent.

The toolkit covers the whole research pipeline — each stage has its tools (every name below is in the toolkit index; the chains are in recipes):

flowchart LR
    A["Start project<br/>/bootstrap-project"] --> B["Get data<br/>data-catalog"]
    B --> C["Analyze<br/>/data-analysis · /stata-replication"]
    C --> D["Figures & tables<br/>real-data-figure · /coef-plot<br/>/build-fragment-table"]
    D --> E["Write<br/>kai-writing · /academic"]
    E --> F["Pre-submission<br/>/review-paper-light → /review-paper<br/>bib-audit · audit-reproducibility"]
    F --> G["Replication package<br/>init-replication · /audit-exhibits"]
    E -.-> H["Talks<br/>research-presentation"]
    E -.-> I["Grants<br/>/review-grant"]

docs.title: Step-by-step install
docs.text: Budget 60–90 minutes the first time. You only do it once per laptop.

docs.title: Step 0 — Things you need before starting
docs.text:
A terminal. This is just a window where you type commands. - Windows: press Win key, type "Terminal", open the app called "Terminal" (or "Windows Terminal"). It opens in PowerShell by default — that's what we'll use. - macOS: press Cmd+Space, type "Terminal", press Enter. - Linux: you already know.

The three lines above are all you need to open a terminal — you don't need to know the difference between "Terminal" and "PowerShell"; either is fine. If the command line is genuinely new and you'd like a gentle 10-minute tour of the handful of commands you'll see (cd, ls, pwd, pasting safely, reading an error), terminal in 10 minutes is there — optional, but it takes the nerves out of every step below.

About admin / root permissions. The install does not require admin / root privileges as a whole. The only step that might prompt for it is npm install -g on macOS/Linux, and Step 1 below tells you how to handle that. On Windows, leave "Add to PATH" ticked in the Node installer and pick "Install for me only" (not "all users") — that avoids any admin prompt.

An Anthropic account with Claude.ai access. Sign up at https://claude.ai/. The Pro plan (currently around 20 USD/month) is enough for normal academic use; the Max plan if you'll run many long sessions. If your team has a shared plan, ask whoever manages it about being added instead of paying personally.

Python 3 (only needed for a couple of plugin hooks, not Claude Code itself). Most macOS/Linux machines already have it; on Windows, install from https://www.python.org/ (tick "Add to PATH") or via Anaconda. Check with python3 --version (or python --version). Any recent 3.x is fine.

A GitHub account, and someone must have invited your GitHub username to the repository. Whoever set up your team's access does this — it doesn't have to be any particular person. Confirm you've accepted the invite before Step 4; without it, Step 4 fails with "repository not found".

Git itself. Windows: install Git for Windows from https://git-scm.com (accept all defaults — this also gives you "Git Bash", a terminal where every command in our docs works). macOS: open Terminal, type git --version; if a pop-up offers to install developer tools, click Install. Without this, Step 4 fails with "git is not recognized".

(Optional) The GitHub CLI for easier GitHub auth. Install from https://cli.github.com. Then run gh auth login once and HTTPS clones won't ask for a password. Skip this if you already use GitHub Desktop or have an SSH key set up.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install Node.js and Claude Code
docs.text:
Claude Code is the command-line tool from Anthropic that everything else runs on top of. It needs Node.js.

  1. Open https://nodejs.org/ and click the "LTS" download button (currently 20.x or 22.x — either works). Run the installer. On Windows, leave "Add to PATH" ticked.
  2. Close and reopen your terminal so it sees the new Node.
  3. Verify Node is installed: 
    node --version
    Should print something like v20.18.0.
  4. Install Claude Code: 
    npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
  5. macOS / Linux: if you see EACCES (permission denied), either rerun with sudo (sudo npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code) OR follow the npm prefix instructions at https://docs.npmjs.com/resolving-eacces-permissions-errors-when-installing-packages-globally.
  6. Windows: should just work; if you see "is not recognized", close and reopen the terminal so Windows picks up the new PATH.
  7. Verify: 
    claude --version

docs.title: Step 2 — Sign in to Claude Code
docs.text:
1. In the terminal, type claude and press Enter.
  2. The first time, it will ask you to sign in. A browser window will pop open. Sign in with the same Anthropic account you used in Step 0. (If you're on a remote machine without a browser, copy the URL it prints and open it on your laptop.)
  3. After the browser shows "success", come back to the terminal — it should say you're signed in.
  4. Type /quit and press Enter to exit. We'll come back later.

docs.title: Step 3 — Install Zotero and the Zotero MCP server
docs.text:
Most people should skip this on the first pass. Zotero powers citation search and bib Path 3 — nothing else. If you're new, or you mainly run Stata/R, or you just want to get going: skip to Step 4 now and come back only if/when you want Zotero-driven citations. (It's also the step most likely to blow the time budget — 20-40 min — and the only one that sends you to an external page.)

Most of our workflows use Zotero (for managing references) and a small bridge program called an MCP server ("MCP" stands for Model Context Protocol — it's just the standard for letting Claude Code talk to outside services). Step-by-step instructions with screenshots-worth-of-detail are in install/mcp-add-zotero.md.

Read that file in full and follow it before moving on. It covers:

  • Installing the Zotero desktop app
  • Generating a Zotero API key (with the exact UI labels)
  • Finding your numeric Zotero user ID
  • Installing uv (a Python package manager — needed because the MCP server is Python)
  • Installing the MCP server itself
  • Registering it with Claude Code
  • Testing it works

When you are invited to a project's Zotero group library, you'll switch to it inside a Claude Code session. That part is also covered in the linked file.

docs.title: Step 4 — Clone this repo
docs.text:
1. Make sure you have been invited to https://github.com/KaliGi/kai-team-claude. Check your email for the invitation, click the link, and accept.
  2. Pick a place on your computer to keep the repo. Anywhere works — common choices are ~/code/, ~/repositories/, or a dedicated Dropbox/github/ folder if you already keep cloned repos there. Cloning into a cloud-synced folder is fine for low-write repos like this one (where you mostly git pull rather than make many local commits); for very active development repos a non-synced folder is slightly safer.
  3. In the terminal, navigate to that location and clone: 
    git clone https://github.com/KaliGi/kai-team-claude.git
cd kai-team-claude
  4. If git asks for a username and password: the simplest beginner path is to install GitHub Desktop (https://desktop.github.com) and sign in once — git in the terminal then reuses its login and never asks again.
  5. Advanced alternative: a fine-grained Personal Access Token (not your GitHub password — GitHub disabled passwords for git over HTTPS in 2021). At https://github.com/settings/tokens?type=beta choose "Only select repositories" → kai-team-claude → Permissions → Contents: Read and write. When you paste it at the password prompt, nothing appears on screen — that's normal; press Enter.
  6. Or run gh auth login once (if you installed the GitHub CLI in Step 0).
  7. Confirm you're inside the cloned folder: 
    pwd
    The output should end in kai-team-claude. Stay in this folder for Step 5.

docs.title: Step 5 — Run the install script
docs.text:
This copies the skills, agents, principles, templates, and docs from the repo into ~/.claude/ (the folder Claude Code reads from on your laptop). If you already have files there, the script backs them up first to ~/.claude/_backup_<timestamp>/ and then replaces them — nothing is lost.

Note: slash commands (/academic, /review-paper, /bootstrap-project, /sync-bib, etc.) are NOT installed by this script. They come from plugins — see Step 6 below.

Make sure your terminal is still in the kai-team-claude folder (Step 4.4 above).

Windows (PowerShell): 

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install\install.ps1
- If PowerShell complains "scripts is disabled on this system", paste this exact line with the -ExecutionPolicy Bypass flag — it's the workaround. - The \ (backslash) in .\install\install.ps1 is correct on Windows.

macOS / Linux: 

bash install/install.sh

You should see "Done." at the end. If anything went wrong, the script prints the error and exits — copy the error and open an issue on the repo (or ask whoever set you up).

docs.title: Step 6 — Register the marketplace, then install the plugins
docs.text:
Slash commands ship via Claude Code's plugin marketplace. One-time install per laptop. These are built-in CLI commands — pasting them costs (almost) no tokens. Paste them exactly; don't describe to Claude what you want it to install:

  1. Close the terminal window completely, then open a fresh one.
  2. Type claude and press Enter, wait for the prompt.
  3. Register the marketplace first (without this, every install below fails with "marketplace not found"). Point it at the repo you cloned in Step 4: 
    /plugin marketplace add ~/kai-team-claude
    (Adjust the path if you cloned somewhere else. Alternative if you prefer pulling straight from GitHub: /plugin marketplace add KaliGi/kai-team-claude — requires your GitHub account to have access to the repo.)
  4. Install the plugins you need (each line is a separate command — type each, press Enter):
Plugin Who needs it Install command project-workflow Everyone — project setup, bibliography, folder hygiene, git help /plugin install project-workflow@kai-team-claude academic-workflow Everyone writing or reviewing papers — drafting, review pipelines, references, data sources /plugin install academic-workflow@kai-team-claude r-research-workflow Anyone running R analyses — regressions, tables, figures, code review /plugin install r-research-workflow@kai-team-claude stata-research-workflow Anyone running Stata — replication scaffolds, esttab tables, code review /plugin install stata-research-workflow@kai-team-claude talks Only if you give research presentations /plugin install talks@kai-team-claude coord Optional, advanced: coordinate YOUR OWN multiple Claude sessions across projects. Never shares data between users. /plugin install coord@kai-team-claude
  1. Restart Claude Code one more time so the plugin registry reloads.

Updating later: see the canonical 4-step ritual in the "Updating later" section below — don't improvise partial updates.

docs.title: Step 7 — Test it works
docs.text:
1. Start Claude Code: claude
  2. Type /academic and press Enter — you should see the academic-writing orchestrator command load. Type /quit to exit.
  3. Try /bootstrap-project next — it should also load.

If /academic or /bootstrap-project doesn't appear, check the plugin install:

  • Windows (PowerShell): Get-Content $env:USERPROFILE\.claude\settings.json | Select-String enabledPlugins -Context 0,10
  • macOS / Linux: grep -A 10 enabledPlugins ~/.claude/settings.json

You should see project-workflow@kai-team-claude and academic-workflow@kai-team-claude in the list. If not, re-run Step 6.

If you have stale bootstrap-project@kai-team-claude or research-pipeline@kai-team-claude entries (those plugins were merged into project-workflow in May 2026 and removed from the marketplace), uninstall them: 

/plugin uninstall bootstrap-project@kai-team-claude
/plugin uninstall research-pipeline@kai-team-claude

Read what you now have. After steps 5-7, your toolkit includes a dozen skills, several slash commands, and four principle docs. The one-page reference is at what-you-have-after-install.md — scan it once so you know what to reach for when.

docs.title: Step 8 — Get added to per-project resources
docs.text:
This is per-project, not per-laptop. For each project, whoever runs it will invite you separately to:

  • A Dropbox folder (the project working directory — papers, code, data, working files)
  • A GitHub repository (the LaTeX source, bib file, and figures)
  • An Overleaf project (only if you'll edit there directly; many predocs skip this and let the Overleaf admin sync between GitHub and Overleaf — only the Overleaf project owner can set up that integration)
  • A Zotero group library (the project's shared references)

Send whoever manages the project the addresses you used for each service so they can invite the right account.

docs.title: Updating later — THE canonical ritual
docs.text:
This is the ONE place the update procedure is defined; other docs link here. The toolkit has two tiers, so updating has exactly four steps — the first two refresh the ~/.claude/ tier (skills, agents, principles), the third refreshes the plugin tier (slash commands), the fourth makes Claude Code reload both:

  1. Pull the repo. Terminal: 
    git -C ~/kai-team-claude pull
    (Adjust the path if you cloned elsewhere.)
  2. Re-run the install script. Terminal:
  3. Windows (PowerShell): powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install\install.ps1
  4. macOS / Linux: bash install/install.sh
  5. Refresh the plugins. Inside Claude Code: 
    /plugin marketplace update kai-team-claude
  6. Restart Claude Code (close the session, start a new one).

Why two tiers? The install script copies files into ~/.claude/ directly; plugins are managed by Claude Code's own registry — neither mechanism updates the other, so both steps are needed. If a plugin still looks stale after step 3, see Troubleshooting ("plugin seems stale").

The install script uses per-item overlay — it replaces just the items the repo contains, leaves any personal items in ~/.claude/ alone, and backs up the previous version of each item it touches to ~/.claude/_backup_<timestamp>/.

Want to preview what the install would change before running it? Run the audit script — it lists what's in your ~/.claude/ vs the repo without making changes:

bash install/audit.sh

It shows three groups: items in both (would be replaced), repo-only items (would be added), and local-only items (would be left alone). Safe to run anytime.

docs.title: Removing the toolkit
docs.text:
Leaving the team or cleaning a machine:

  1. Inside Claude Code: /plugin uninstall <name>@kai-team-claude for each installed plugin (list them with /plugin).
  2. Remove the Zotero bridge if you added it: claude mcp remove zotero.
  3. Delete the items the install script placed in ~/.claude/ (skills/, agents/, principles/, templates/, docs/ — run bash install/audit.sh first to see exactly what's repo-managed vs yours; backups live in ~/.claude/_backup_<timestamp>/).
  4. Delete your clone of this repo, and revoke the Zotero API key + GitHub access token in the respective web UIs.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"command not found: claude" — Node.js install probably didn't add npm's global folder to your PATH. - Windows: close and reopen the terminal so it picks up the new PATH; if still broken, check that node --version works first. - macOS / Linux: run npm config get prefix to find where npm puts global packages (e.g., /usr/local). Then add export PATH="$(npm config get prefix)/bin:$PATH" to your shell profile (~/.zshrc on modern macOS, ~/.bashrc on Linux), close the terminal, reopen.

"command not found: uvx" / "uv" — uv adds itself to PATH only in newly-opened terminals after install. Open a new terminal and try again.

"npm install -g" fails with EACCES (macOS / Linux) — see Step 1.4 above.

A plugin seems stale after /plugin marketplace update — the clean refresh is uninstall + reinstall: /plugin uninstall <name>@kai-team-claude then /plugin install <name>@kai-team-claude, then restart. (Only needed when the marketplace update didn't propagate; not part of the normal ritual.)

/academic doesn't appear in Claude Code — the plugin isn't installed or enabled (slash commands ship via plugins, NOT via the install script). Inside Claude Code run /plugin, confirm academic-workflow@kai-team-claude is listed and enabled; if not, redo Step 6 (marketplace add, then install), then restart Claude Code.

Skills fire but the principles file is missing — agents look up ~/.claude/principles/academic-writing.md. If that path doesn't exist on your machine, the install script didn't copy principles/ correctly. Re-run the install script.

Zotero MCP errors out — the Zotero desktop app must be running for the MCP server to talk to it. Open Zotero and try again.

git clone says "repository not found" — you have not been invited to the repository yet, or you accepted the invite with a different account. Ask whoever set up your access to (re-)invite the GitHub username you're cloning with.

uv install on Windows blocked by IT policy — the irm | iex one-liner can be blocked. Download the installer manually from https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases and run the .msi file.

Anything else — open an Issue on this repo (https://github.com/KaliGi/kai-team-claude/issues) or ask whoever set you up. Include the exact error text and what step you were on.

docs.title: Installed? Here's where to go next
docs.text:
• Brand new to the toolkit? → What the toolkit is, then First things to try for a quick win.
  • Want the full catalogue? → What's inside · How to do a task (recipes).
  • Here to work on a shared paper? → the Working together section: the co-author quickstart.
  • Or go back to the Home page and pick a section.

docs.title: Maintainer notes (for repo owners and people who edit kai-team-claude)
docs.text: This file is for anyone who pushes to the repo — initially Kai, eventually trusted co-authors with PR access. Predocs and read-only collaborators can skip it.

docs.title: Principle: what goes in the repo, what stays in ~/.claude/
docs.text:
A skill / agent / command goes in kai-team-claude if it is:

  • Necessary for team members working on shared papers (would they actually use it?), AND
  • Mature enough to be a stable interface (not a half-finished prototype), OR
  • Pure infrastructure that other items depend on (e.g., agents called by commands).

A skill / agent / command stays in ~/.claude/ only (never in the repo) if it is:

  • A personal experiment or prototype not yet ready for others
  • Specific to a project the rest of the team isn't on (e.g., something for a consulting engagement nobody else is involved in)
  • Project-internal output you don't want others to see (e.g., a skill that contains sensitive review notes)
  • Something whose value is purely speculative — keep it private until proven

When in doubt: err on the side of keeping it local first, share later. It's trivial to add a polished local item to the repo (one cp and a commit). It's much harder to retroactively remove or hide an item that's already public.

docs.title: How personal items are protected
docs.text:
The install scripts (install.ps1, install.sh) use per-item overlay logic:

  • For each item the repo contains (e.g., skills/kai-writing/), the install script replaces just that one in ~/.claude/.
  • Items in ~/.claude/ that are not named in the repo are left alone.

Concretely, if your ~/.claude/skills/ contains:

adversarial-review/         (also in repo)
kai-writing/                (also in repo)
real-data-figure/           (also in repo)
research-presentation/      (also in repo)
tikz-figure/                (also in repo)
_my-private-experiment/     (NOT in repo — local-only)
scientific-writing-analysis-SKILL.md  (NOT in repo — using Anthropic plugin instead)

Running bash install/install.sh after git pull will: - Replace the five items that are in the repo (with backup of previous versions) - Leave _my-private-experiment/ and scientific-writing-analysis-SKILL.md alone

So you can safely accumulate personal items in ~/.claude/ without worrying about the install script wiping them.

docs.title: Naming convention for local-only items
docs.text:
To make local-only items obvious in directory listings (and to avoid future collisions with new repo items), prefix them with _ (underscore):

~/.claude/skills/_my-experiment/
~/.claude/agents/_personal-helper.md
~/.claude/commands/_private-shortcut.md

This isn't enforced anywhere, just a hygiene convention.

docs.title: Auditing what's where
docs.text:
Run the audit script to see, at a glance, what's in your ~/.claude/ vs the repo:

bash install/audit.sh

Output groups items into three buckets: - In both — these will be replaced on the next install - Local-only — these will be left alone (your personal items) - Repo-only — these will be added on the next install

This is the safest way to preview a git pull && install before running it.

docs.title: Adding a new item to the repo
docs.text:
If you've polished a personal skill / agent / command and want to share it:

  1. Decide if it really belongs in the repo. Apply the principle above.
  2. Copy from ~/.claude/ into the repo working copy. 
    cp -r ~/.claude/skills/<name>/ ~/code/kai-team-claude/skills/
    (Or for an agent / command: copy the single .md file.)
  3. Read through the file for personal references that shouldn't be public — project paths, draft notes, references to specific people who aren't on the team.
  4. Sanitize anything inappropriate. If the item references Kai's voice or team conventions, that's fine; if it references a specific manuscript or review note, redact.
  5. Commit and push with a descriptive message: 
    cd ~/code/kai-team-claude
git add skills/<name>          # explicit path — never `git add -A` or `git add .`
git commit -m "skills/<name>: add <one-line description>"
git push                       # ask before pushing (see git-workflow rule)
  6. Tell the team so they git pull && install.

docs.title: Removing an item from the repo
docs.text:
Sometimes a shared item turns out to be too project-specific or has been replaced by an Anthropic plugin (e.g., scientific-writing-analysis). To remove:

  1. git rm -r the item in the repo working copy.
  2. Commit and push with a clear message: 
    git rm -r skills/<name>
git commit -m "skills/<name>: remove (now provided by <plugin/replacement>)"
git push
