  3. Note: removing from the repo does not delete it from collaborators' ~/.claude/. Their local copies stay until they manually delete them. That's usually what you want (no surprise deletions on git pull).

docs.title: Editing an item that's in the repo
docs.text:
Edit it in the repo working copy at ~/code/kai-team-claude/, then push. Don't edit in ~/.claude/ first — that creates two sources of truth and you'll forget which one is current.

If you want to test a change locally before pushing:

# edit the file in ~/code/kai-team-claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
cp ~/code/kai-team-claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
# test in a Claude Code session
# if good, commit and push
cd ~/code/kai-team-claude && git add skills/<name>/SKILL.md && git commit -m "..." && git push

docs.title: Sanitization checklist before pushing
docs.text:
Before any git push to a public-ish repo (even private with several collaborators):

  • [ ] No absolute paths like C:/Users/<name>/... — use ~/... or relative paths
  • [ ] No hardcoded API keys, tokens, or credentials
  • [ ] No project-internal manuscript IDs (e.g., journal submission numbers)
  • [ ] No personal email addresses other than the maintainer's
  • [ ] No references to specific reviewers, collaborators outside the team, or private project decisions
  • [ ] References to style profiles and team conventions are fine and expected

If unsure: open an Issue rather than push, ask Kai.

docs.title: Cutting a release (versioning)
docs.text:
The kit uses two version levels — see "How versioning works" on the Updates page for the rationale. As a maintainer you touch both:

  1. Per-plugin semver. When you change a plugin's behaviour, bump its plugin.json version (major.minor.patch) in the same commit. Patch = fix, minor = additive feature, major = breaking change.
  2. Add a changelog entry. Put a dated ## YYYY-MM-DD — <headline> block at the top of the root CHANGELOG.md describing what changed and, briefly, why. This is the single source of truth — the site's Updates page pulls it in at build time via a snippet include, so never duplicate it into docs/.
  3. Roll the CalVer cut when the month turns (or when a batch of changes is meaningfully a new vintage): edit the root /VERSION file to the new YYYY.MM. That's the version people quote when they ask "are we on the same conventions?".
  4. Run the gate before pushing: RUN_HARNESS=1 bash scripts/release_check.sh (INDEX freshness, recipe tokens, canonical-mirror sync, the 00_setup harness, and the mkdocs build). Push only when it's green.

docs.title: The manual workflow (by hand, no AI required)
docs.text: Why this page exists. Nothing in this setup requires Claude Code. The folder structure, the git flow, the Overleaf sync — all of it is plain, ordinary tooling you can drive entirely by hand. Claude is a convenience that removes typing and remembers the rules for you; it is not a dependency. If you prefer to work manually, want to save tokens, or are simply more comfortable in your own terminal, this page is the complete by-hand path. The structure is deliberately compatible with manual coding — you can mix: do the prose by hand, let Claude generate a figure, commit yourself.

docs.title: The golden rule: one writer per file at a time
docs.text:
Every other rule is downstream of this one. Two people editing the same file at the same time is the root cause of nearly every collaboration disaster — Dropbox conflicted-copies, git merge conflicts, lost edits. The whole structure exists to make "one writer per file" the natural state:

  • You work in your own clone, so your working copies are yours alone.
  • Shared things that genuinely have one owner (the bibliography, the Overleaf project) have one designated person who writes them; everyone else proposes changes through that person or through a pull request.

If you remember nothing else, remember: before you edit a shared file, make sure you're the only one editing it.

docs.title: Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence
docs.text:
The single most common confusion. A file being visible in your Dropbox folder does not mean it is in git. They are two independent systems:

Dropbox git What it syncs every file in the folder, instantly only what you git add + commit + push What it's for backup, seeing each other's folders history, merging, the canonical main A new file appears automatically, everywhere only after you commit and push it

So a file can be sitting in Dropbox, synced to everyone, and still be completely absent from git history. That's fine for scratch notes — but for anything that belongs to the project (code, paper text, figures), "it's in Dropbox" is not "it's saved properly". It has to be committed and pushed to be part of the real record.

docs.title: The Overleaf ↔ git ↔ Dropbox triangle
docs.text:
On Overleaf-mastered papers there are three places a file can live, and the sync between Overleaf and git is manual — there is no magic bridge keeping them aligned. This is the part that trips people up, so here it is explicitly:

flowchart LR
    OL["Overleaf<br/>(where prose is written)"]
    DBX["Dropbox folder<br/>(backup + sharing)"]
    GIT[("git / GitHub main<br/>(history + canonical record)")]
    OL -. "manual sync via Overleaf's git: push / pull" .-> GIT
    GIT -. "manual sync via Overleaf's git: push / pull" .-> OL
    GIT -- "auto, via your clone" --> DBX
    DBX -- "auto" --> GIT

The standard: keep git the source of truth. git holds the canonical record, so whatever is authoritative has to reach git. On Overleaf-mastered papers that means syncing Overleaf ↔ git through Overleaf's own git access (push/pull), not by shuffling files around. Dropbox then updates itself, because your clone lives inside it — you don't manage Dropbox by hand at all.

The anti-pattern to avoid: writing in Overleaf and then copying the .tex (or a PDF) into the Dropbox folder by hand. It looks like it works — Dropbox and Overleaf match — but git silently falls behind (Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence), and you now have two diverging copies of a file that lives in git. If hand-copying has been your team's habit, that's a common mistake with a clean fix — see common issues.

Two corollaries that prevent the nastiest tangles:

  • Figures travel one way: code → git → Overleaf. A figure is generated by a script, committed to git, and then pulled/uploaded into Overleaf. Never "fix" a figure inside Overleaf — the next regeneration overwrites it and the source-of-truth (the script) never learned about your change.
  • Never hand-copy a file that also lives in git. If a file is tracked in git, edit it through git and let it flow — copying it by hand around git creates two diverging versions of the same thing, which is exactly the conflict you're trying to avoid.

docs.title: Doing the core tasks by hand
docs.text:
Each of these is a normal git operation. The full, illustrated runbook is in the setup walkthrough and per-project onboarding; the short version:

Task By hand Set up your clone git clone <repo> clone_<XX> inside the Dropbox folder, then touch .data-in-parent (why) Start work cd clone_<XX>, git checkout -b <XX>/<topic> Save a checkpoint git add <file> (explicit paths — never git add -A), git commit -m "..." Share it git push, then open a pull request on GitHub Get others' merged work git fetch origin && git merge origin/main Merge a PR review on GitHub, then merge (anyone can — there's no lead)

The one habit the structure asks of you is in the first row: work inside your clone_<XX>/, never at the shared container root. Why that matters is the whole of why collaboration is hard.

docs.title: When to let Claude do it instead
docs.text: Everything above, Claude Code can do for you — and it remembers the rules (explicit git add paths, "push asks first", commit-message hygiene) so you don't have to. The trade is tokens and a little trust. A reasonable middle: do the parts you're confident in by hand, and ask Claude for the parts you'd otherwise have to look up. Each task page in this site shows both paths — the manual commands and the one-line Claude request — so you can pick per task, not once-and-for-all.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text: If you've never used Claude Code, start here — it's a five-minute orientation, then pointers to the best existing guides (no need for us to re-write what Anthropic already documents well).

docs.title: What it is, in one line
docs.text: Claude Code is Anthropic's AI assistant that runs in your terminal (or as a desktop app / IDE extension) and can actually read, edit, and run files in your project — not just chat about them. If that distinction is new, read our short How Claude Code thinks — it explains "chat vs. a harness" and, importantly, that you approve every action; it's not autopilot.

docs.title: Get started (external, official)
docs.text:
• Official quickstart — the canonical getting-started guide from Anthropic: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/quickstart. It covers signing in, your first session, and the basic commands. You need a terminal, a project folder, and a Claude subscription (Pro/Max/Team).
  • It also runs on the web, as a desktop app, and inside VS Code / JetBrains — the quickstart lists all of them.

docs.title: Then, for our setup
docs.text:
Once Claude Code itself works, the toolkit (our skills + plugins for economics-paper work) installs on top:

  • What the toolkit is — skills, plugins, the marketplace.
  • Install the Claude Code toolkit — our step-by-step, cross-platform, copy-paste install (this is the one to follow for this kit).
  • First things to try — a useful result in five minutes.

New to terminals too? The terminal in 10 minutes primer removes the nerves first.

docs.title: LaTeX
docs.text: Much of this kit assumes your paper is written in LaTeX, and several pages say "you can just compile it locally." If LaTeX is unfamiliar — or you've always used Word — here's what it is, why it's worth it (especially now, with AI), and how to set it up locally so you can produce a PDF without any online service.

docs.title: What LaTeX is
docs.text: LaTeX is a typesetting system for documents. Instead of formatting by hand as you type (Word), you write plain text with light markup — \section{...}, \cite{...}, an equation between $ … $ — and a compiler turns it into a polished PDF with consistent maths, references, and layout. The source is just text files (paper.tex, references.bib), which is what makes everything else in this kit work.

docs.title: Why LaTeX — especially now, with AI
docs.text:
• Git and an AI assistant both work best on plain text. Because the source is text, git shows you a clean line-by-line history of every change, and Claude Code can read and edit the .tex directly — neither works well on Word's binary files.
  • The old downside is mostly gone. LaTeX's reputation for fiddly syntax was the main reason to avoid it. With an LLM writing and fixing the markup for you, that cost largely disappears — you describe what you want, it produces correct LaTeX.
  • Professional output for free. Maths, cross-references, bibliographies, and tables come out consistent and reproducible, the same every time.
  • Word is still fine if you prefer it — but you give up clean git diffs, smooth AI editing, and the Overleaf track-changes workflow. For a paper that several people and an agent will all edit, LaTeX pays off.

docs.title: Local setup — so you can compile without Overleaf
docs.text:
You don't need Overleaf to use LaTeX; install a TeX distribution once and you can compile on your own machine, offline. Install the distribution for your OS (these are the standard installers — follow their own instructions, nothing to copy from here):

  • Windows: MiKTeX — installs missing packages on demand.
  • macOS: MacTeX.
  • Linux / cross-platform: TeX Live.

An editor helps but isn't required: VS Code with the LaTeX Workshop extension, or TeXstudio — or just compile from the terminal. Once installed, building a PDF is one command in the paper folder:

latexmk -pdf paper.tex

docs.title: LaTeX vs. Overleaf — use either
docs.text: Overleaf compiles in the browser (no local install) and adds track-changes review of prose. Local LaTeX is free, works offline, and integrates directly with git and Claude Code. Many people use both — local for day-to-day editing, Overleaf when a co-author wants to mark up the text. (Overleaf's track changes and git sync are paid-plan features the project owner sets up — see New to Overleaf?.) Which you need is part of choosing your setup.

docs.title: Overleaf
docs.text: Overleaf is a browser-based editor for LaTeX — the typesetting system most economics papers are written in. It's where a lot of co-authors do their actual writing. If you've never used it, this is a short orientation plus the best existing tutorials (Overleaf's own are excellent; no point re-writing them).

docs.title: What it is, in one line
docs.text: Overleaf = write LaTeX in your browser, see the compiled PDF next to it, with several co-authors editing the same document. No local LaTeX install needed to start.

docs.title: Do you even need Overleaf? (often no)
docs.text:
Worth saying up front: Overleaf is optional. Everything in a paper compiles locally — latexmk -pdf paper.tex (or your editor's build button) produces the same PDF on your own machine, with no browser and no account. The git- mastered mode keeps paper.tex in git and never touches Overleaf at all.

The one genuine reason to use Overleaf is track changes — the review/suggesting mode where co-authors mark edits and comments on the prose in the browser and you accept/reject them, the way you would in Word. If your team doesn't need track changes, you can skip Overleaf entirely and compile locally — it's one less moving part. Choose Overleaf for the track-changes review, not out of habit.

docs.title: Learn it (external, from Overleaf)
docs.text:
• Learn LaTeX in 30 minutes — the standard beginner tutorial; assumes zero prior LaTeX and walks you through your first document (titles, math, lists, tables, references): https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Learn_LaTeX_in_30_minutes.
  • More tutorials (figures, bibliographies, tables, beamer slides): https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Tutorials.

docs.title: How Overleaf fits our workflow
docs.text:
This is the part specific to collaborating with this setup:

  • On Overleaf-mastered papers, the prose lives in Overleaf and everything else (code, figures, the bibliography) lives in git. One person is the Overleaf admin (only the Overleaf project owner can set up the Overleaf↔git sync).
  • The bibliography (references.bib) and figures travel code → git → Overleaf, not the other way. Don't hand-copy files that also live in git — keep git the source of truth. The why and the mechanics are in the manual workflow and common issues.

docs.title: Setting it up — the Overleaf owner does this once, first
docs.text:
If a project will use Overleaf, the project owner sets up the Overleaf↔git link, and it's worth doing this first, because it's what connects Overleaf to the GitHub repo — once that link exists, everyone else just clones from GitHub into their folder as usual.

  1. Owner: create (or open) the Overleaf project. In Overleaf, open Menu → Sync → GitHub (or Git) and link it to the project's GitHub repository. (Overleaf's GitHub/Git sync is a paid-plan feature — if Menu → Sync has no Git/GitHub option, the plan doesn't include it; fall back to git-mastered mode and compile locally.)
  2. From then on, syncing Overleaf ↔ git is a manual push/pull through that link — there's no live bridge. The owner (or whoever holds the Overleaf admin role) does the sync so two people don't push conflicting versions.
  3. Everyone else: never set up their own Overleaf↔git link — they clone the GitHub repo into their Dropbox folder (set up your working clone) and edit prose in Overleaf via the browser. Code, figures, and the bibliography still travel code → git → Overleaf.

(Step-by-step for the routine push/pull cycle is on the roadmap; for now the owner uses Overleaf's own Git/GitHub menu to push and pull.)

Not every project uses Overleaf — git-mastered papers keep the .tex in git directly, compiled locally. Which mode a project uses is declared in its CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Why structure matters (even solo)
docs.text: This page is tool-agnostic. It's about how to organize an empirical research project so it stays sane over years — no AI, no special software assumed. The toolkit automates a lot of it later, but the principles below stand entirely on their own, and they're worth following even if you work alone in a plain folder.

docs.title: Why structure at all — even working solo
docs.text: The person most likely to need your project organized is future-you, six months from now, reopening it for a revision. A predictable structure means you can answer, instantly: where's the raw data? which script made Figure 3? which file is the current draft? Without that, every reopening starts with archaeology. So the payoff isn't bureaucratic tidiness — it's that the project stays reproducible and resumable by you, and later by anyone else.

docs.title: The principles (the part that doesn't depend on any tool)
docs.text:
1. Separate raw from processed, and never edit raw. The data exactly as you obtained it is the one thing you can't regenerate. Keep it read-only; build everything else from it with code. If a cleaning step was wrong, you fix the code and re-run — the ground truth is untouched.
  2. Code is the source of every exhibit. Each figure, table, and number in the paper should come from a script you can re-run, not from a one-off you can't reconstruct. "Reproducible" just means: delete output/, run the code, get it back.
  3. One canonical file per artefact. No analysis_v2.do, final_FINAL.tex. One 02_analysis file, one paper.tex — history lives in version control (below) or dated archive copies, not in the filename.
  4. A runnable pipeline. Number your scripts so the project runs top to bottom (00_setup → 01_cleaning → 02_analysis → 99_run_all), with one setup file owning all paths so nothing is hard-coded to your machine.
  5. Write down what isn't obvious. A short codebook / data dictionary and a README turn "what was this variable again?" into a lookup.

That's the whole core. The concrete folder map that implements it is what goes where; the deeper rationale is the ideas behind it. A standard, reproducible structure is also exactly what a replication package needs — so if you work this way, the package is almost free.

docs.title: Required vs. recommended
docs.text:
Not everything here carries equal weight, and it's worth being honest about which is which — so nobody feels bossed into preferences, and nobody treats a genuinely load-bearing rule as optional.

Required — break these and something real goes wrong:

  • Never overwrite or edit raw data. It's the one thing you can't get back.
  • To share work, commit and push it to git. Saving (Dropbox) is not sharing; the canonical record is git. (Solo with no git, this doesn't apply.)
  • One writer per file at a time (on a team) — two people editing the same file means one silently loses their work.
  • Exhibits trace to code. A number or figure you can't regenerate from a script isn't reproducible — and reproducibility is the credibility floor.

Recommended — sensible defaults you can adapt:

  • The exact folder layout and names (what goes where) — a working solution, not the only one; what matters is everyone uses the same.
  • Keeping clones inside Dropbox, using Overleaf, using Claude Code or the toolkit, the specific multi-clone setup — all genuinely optional choices. Pick what fits; the required rules above hold either way.

When in doubt: the required list is short on purpose. Everything else is a default you're free to change.

docs.title: Working alone vs. with others — and where git comes in
docs.text:
Working solo, the principles above plus a tidy folder are most of what you need. Version control (git) is helpful even then — it gives you a timeline you can roll back and a record of why each change happened — but you can get a long way with disciplined folders and the occasional dated backup.

The calculus changes the moment more than one actor edits the project — and today that's not just co-authors:

  • Co-authors edit in parallel. Without version control, two people changing the same file means one silently overwrites the other (the classic Dropbox "conflicted copy").
  • AI agents — Claude Code, Codex — make many edits quickly. That's a huge speed-up, but it's also a lot of changes to a lot of files. You want each one to be a reviewable diff you can inspect and undo, not a silent mutation. Git is what turns "the AI changed twelve files" into "here's exactly what it changed, keep or revert each."

So the rule of thumb:

You're working… What you need Alone, by hand the folder principles above; git optional but nice Alone, with an AI agent the principles + git — so every agent edit is a reviewable, revertible diff With co-authors (± agents) the principles + git + a collaboration setup so parallel work merges instead of clobbering

The more hands on the project — human or AI — the more git earns its keep. The folder principles are the foundation either way; git is what lets several actors build on that foundation at once without stepping on each other. How that collaboration setup works is Working together; why the AI agents are safe to let loose on a git-backed project is how Claude Code thinks.

docs.title: Set up your working clone
docs.text:
Why this page. Joining a shared project means a handful of one-time access steps — folder, repo, bibliography, and (sometimes) Overleaf. Doing them once, in the right order, is what lets everything afterwards "just work". This page is that runbook; whoever set the project up sends it to you with the project-specific details filled in.

Two roles — make sure you're reading the right one.

  • Setting up the project for the first time (or migrating an existing one to the shared layout)? That's a one-time job for one person — see the setup walkthrough and run /bootstrap-project (new project) or /refactor-structure --migrate-to-multi-clone (existing one). You create the container + your own clone, push main to GitHub, and invite everyone else as collaborators.
  • Joining a project someone else already set up? This page is for you — you receive a few invitations and create your own working clone.

Once your laptop is set up (see the main README.md for the one-time install), each project you join needs a few separate access invitations.

docs.title: Before you start — the accounts and tools you need
docs.text:
Four things must be in place before the clone steps below will work. The first two are the ones people most often miss, and the organizer cannot do them for you:

  1. Your own GitHub account, added as a collaborator on the repo. The repo is private, so without a GitHub account and an accepted collaborator invite you cannot clone it or push to it. Create one free at github.com, then send the organizer your GitHub username/email (below) so they can invite you.
  2. Git installed on your machine — the git program itself. On Windows, install Git for Windows (it also signs you in to GitHub via a browser pop-up the first time); macOS/Linux usually already have git.
  3. The Dropbox container shared with you (accept the share) so the project folder syncs to your machine.
  4. Only if you'll use Claude Code to do the setup: Claude Code installed + a Claude subscription. Two things happen the first time, both normal and worth expecting:
  5. Claude asks permission before it runs a git command. When you ask it to set up your clone, it pauses and asks you to approve each command (e.g. git clone …) — say yes (you can allow git for the whole session). It never runs git silently.
  6. The first clone or push asks you to sign in to GitHub — a browser window opens to log in once. (If it asks for a "password" instead, paste a Personal Access Token, not your account password; the screen stays blank as you paste — that's expected.) It's remembered afterwards.

docs.title: What to send the organizer
docs.text:
For each new project, send whoever set the project up the email address you use for each of these services. They'll send invitations against those exact addresses.

  • Dropbox account email
  • GitHub account email (or username)
  • Overleaf account email (only if you'll edit there directly; many people skip this)
  • Zotero account email

docs.title: What you'll receive
docs.text: For each project, expect four invitations:

docs.title: 1. Dropbox folder
docs.text:
The project's Dropbox folder is the working directory — it contains the LaTeX source, data, code, working drafts, and a CLAUDE.md file that tells Claude Code about the project's conventions and style rules. Once invited, the folder shows up in your Dropbox client and syncs continuously.

When you start Claude Code from inside the project folder, it automatically reads CLAUDE.md, so the session knows about the project conventions.

docs.title: 2. GitHub repository
docs.text:
The GitHub repo holds the LaTeX source (*.tex), the bibliography (*.bib), and figures. Whether GitHub or Overleaf is canonical depends on the project's mode — which is declared in the project's CLAUDE.md (## Project mode section). The four modes (Overleaf-mastered, Git-mastered-no-bridge, Git-mastered-with-bridge, Personal-scratch) are defined in principles/project-structure-canonical.md — read that as the source of truth before working in the repo.

Workflow: - For bibliography updates, follow principles/bibliography-and-literature.md. Do NOT hand-edit the ZOTERO zone of references.bib — those edits are overwritten on /sync-bib. Add citations via Path 1 (just type \citep{...} in .tex), Path 2 (hand-add to the MANUAL zone), or Path 3 (Zotero Connector + /sync-bib). See docs/co-author-onboarding.md for the short version. - For paper text edits, the rule depends on project mode: - Overleaf-mastered: drafting happens locally; the Overleaf admin applies final changes manually in Overleaf. Claude does NOT commit or push .tex content without explicit per-session approval. - Git-mastered: draft directly in the master .tex files; git provides version history. Pushes still ask per principles/git-workflow.md.

docs.title: 3. Overleaf project
docs.text: Optional. Many teams keep Overleaf as the writing surface of last resort and have collaborators work in the Dropbox working/ folder. If you are invited to Overleaf, treat it as read-only unless the Overleaf admin says otherwise.

docs.title: 4. Zotero group library
docs.text:
Each project usually has its own Zotero group library — separate from your personal Zotero. After you accept the invitation, switch to the group library inside a Claude Code session by saying "switch to group library " — whoever manages the project's Zotero library will give you the ID.

The group library is the source of truth for citations. New citations get added to the group library first, then a Claude Code session converts the entry to BibTeX and appends it to the project's .bib file in the GitHub repo.

docs.title: Set up your own working clone (multi-clone projects)
docs.text:
Skip this section if the project's CLAUDE.md has no ## Multi-clone layout block — then you work directly in the shared Dropbox folder per the Quick-start below.

"But I don't have a clone yet — where do I open Claude Code?" This is the one apparent exception to the open-in-your-clone rule, and it trips every new co-author. You don't need your clone to exist to create it — you create it by cloning from GitHub. So for this one-time setup only, open your terminal (or a Claude Code session) at the container (the shared Dropbox project folder). Once your clone_<XX>/ exists, every session opens inside it as usual. Two accesses must be in place first: the Dropbox container shared with you, and GitHub collaborator access on the repo. (Or just open at the container and ask Claude Code: "set up my working clone, my initials are MC.")

On multi-clone projects, each co-author works in their own nested git clone inside the Dropbox project folder. The project root is a shared container, not a git repo — there is no "lead" and no canonical root clone, and everyone is equal. You never run git at the root; all your git work happens inside your own clone_<XX>/. Full rationale: principles/project-structure-canonical.md, Multi-clone pattern.

The single most important fact: cloning does NOT give you the data. data/raw and data/processed are gitignored — the one canonical data copy lives in the parent Dropbox folder. The .data-in-parent marker (step 5 below) makes your clone's scripts find it.

Two ways to do it — pick one:

  • Ask Claude Code (easiest). Open a session at the container (see the box above) and say: "Set up my working clone — my initials are AW." It runs the commands below for you, pausing to ask you to approve each git command (say yes), and the first git clone triggers the GitHub sign-in described in "Before you start." You stay hands-off after approving.
  • By hand. Run the ~6 commands yourself. Replace AW/aw with your two-letter initials (the ones in the project CLAUDE.md ## Collaborators table). Works the same in Git Bash, PowerShell, or macOS Terminal:
# 1. Go to the Dropbox project folder
cd "<path-to-Dropbox>/<project>"

# 2. Clone the repo into your per-author folder
#    (someone must have added you as a GitHub collaborator first)
git clone https://github.com/KaliGi/<repo>.git clone_AW

# 3. Enter it, create your branch, and publish it — never work on main
cd clone_AW
git checkout -b AW/exp-sandbox
git push -u origin AW/exp-sandbox   # publish the branch; enables plain `git push`/`git pull` later

# 4. Tell the pipeline that data lives in the parent folder
touch .data-in-parent          # PowerShell: New-Item .data-in-parent -ItemType File

# 4b. Drop the "this is your copy, you can't break it" note into your clone
#     so the foreign files don't alarm you (and gitignore it — it's personal).
cp ../<path-to-kai-team-claude>/templates/clone-readme.md ./README.md
#    (Or just ask Claude Code: "add the clone README to my clone.")

# 4c. Install the paper-PDF hook, so that every time you pull a merge into
#     your clone the container's paper/ folder gets a freshly compiled PDF of
#     main (one obvious place to grab the current paper at submission time —
#     see "The current paper PDF at the container" below). Then run it once to
#     populate the container the first time.
cp ../<path-to-kai-team-claude>/templates/hooks/post-merge-paper .git/hooks/post-merge
chmod +x .git/hooks/post-merge
sh .git/hooks/post-merge            # first-time populate (safe to re-run)
#    (Or just ask Claude Code: "install the paper-PDF merge hook in my clone.")

# 5. Verify: run the setup script — the banner must show your branch
#    and the rawdata/processed paths must point at ../data/
#    (Windows often doesn't have Rscript/python on PATH — use the full
#    executable paths from the project CLAUDE.md if the bare name fails.)
Rscript code/00_setup.R
#    Stata:  "C:\Program Files\StataNow19\StataSE-64.exe" /e do code/00_setup.do
#    Python: python code/00_setup.py

From now on, every session (Claude Code, R, Stata) starts inside clone_AW/ — never in the parent. Your code, paper edits, and exhibits live on your branch and reach the team via git push + pull request.

docs.title: The current paper PDF at the container
docs.text:
Once the hook (step 4c) is installed, the container holds a paper/ folder with the compiled PDF of main. Every time anyone pulls a merge into their clone (git merge origin/main), the hook recompiles main's paper and drops the fresh PDF there. This is the one place to grab the current paper — e.g. at submission time — without opening anyone's clone. It holds only the PDF, not the sources or outputs: every clone already has those from main, so the container deliberately doesn't duplicate them.

A PAPER_README.md sits next to it: do not edit there — the PDF is regenerated on the next merge and is not in git; all real work happens in your clone and reaches main through a PR. The hook is best-effort: if your machine has no LaTeX or the paper can't bare-compile (e.g. it uses \includepdf), it skips silently and leaves the previous PDF rather than breaking your merge — so refresh happens on whichever machine can compile main cleanly.

docs.title: Working in your clone — the two-step session setup
docs.text:
Why this matters: Claude Code acts on the folder you open it in. Open it in your clone and your work lands on your branch; open it in the parent and it would touch the shared container directly. So a co-author session is always:

  1. Open Claude Code in your clone folder (clone_AW/). Desktop app: Open folder → pick clone_AW/. Terminal: cd clone_AW && claude. This is where your git work happens (your branch).
  2. Add the parent folder only if you need Claude to read or add shared files at the project root — the shared data/, literature/, or project_management/. Desktop app: Add another folder → pick the project root. You do NOT need this just to run your code — your scripts already reach the shared data/ on their own through the .data-in-parent re-anchor; step 2 is only for when Claude itself should read/add a shared file (e.g. "save this PDF to literature/").

What Claude Code asks when you add the parent. It will ask whether the added folder is a git working directory or just a folder to read/write. Answer "just a folder" (a plain added directory) — the parent is the shared container, not a git repo, so there's no git there to manage. Your git stays entirely in your clone_<XX>/. (If you accidentally say it's a git directory, nothing breaks — the container has no .git, so Claude simply finds nothing to act on.)

Two cautions when the parent is added: (a) only read or add shared resources (data/, literature/, project_management/) — never reach into another person's clone_<XX>/, that's theirs; (b) anything tracked or structural (code, paper, reorganizing folders) goes through your branch and a merge, not by editing the parent directly. Reading shared files and adding literature/notes is fine; the one thing to flag to the team first is overwriting shared data/processed/ (two people can clobber it).

When your branch produces its first exhibit: copy kai-team-claude/templates/exhibits-note.tex to your clone root and add every exhibit to it as you create it (finding-style section title, a 2-4 sentence interpretation, consistent wording, a transition sentence, \FloatBarrier after each — all scaffolded in the template). Compile with latexmk -pdf exhibits-note.tex from the clone root. This one PDF is how the team reviews your branch's work; full rules in the co-author handbook §2.6 step 6.

Keeping your branch current (do this every few days, and always before opening a PR): your clone is pinned to your branch, so plain git pull only fetches your own branch — it will say "up to date" even when main has moved on for weeks. Pull main in explicitly:

git fetch origin
git merge origin/main          # brings the team's merged work into your branch
# resolve any conflicts, then: git push

Notes: - Your clone syncs via Dropbox like everything else — unpushed work is backed up. Do NOT mark it Dropbox-ignored and do NOT create junctions or symlinks inside it. - If you are a disciplined daily-pusher and prefer a clone outside Dropbox entirely, that variant is supported — see the canonical spec ("Placement"). Be aware: Dropbox does not back that clone up. - One-time at project bootstrap (whoever sets the project up, once): clone_*/ in the root .gitignore, the CLAUDE.md multi-clone block, GitHub collaborator access. It's a chore, not an authority.

docs.title: Quick-start: your first Claude Code session on the project
docs.text:
1. Open a terminal and cd into the project's Dropbox folder — or into your clone_<XX>/ clone if the project is multi-clone (see the section above).
  2. Pull the latest content for the project's mode:
  3. Git-mastered project: git pull — in your own clone on multi-clone projects; at the Dropbox project root only on single-clone projects (or in the github-sync/ sub-folder if the project uses that legacy mirror layout).
  4. Overleaf-mastered project: there is no pull step from a Claude Code session — the canonical source is Overleaf. The Overleaf admin's latest manual application of edits arrives via Dropbox sync. Check paper/ for the newest date-stamped PDF.

If unsure which mode applies, read the ## Project mode section of the project's CLAUDE.md. The four modes are defined in principles/project-structure-canonical.md. 3. Start Claude Code: claude. 4. The first thing Claude Code does is read CLAUDE.md — wait for that to finish. 5. You can now ask things like: - "Read the introduction and tell me what it argues" - "What's on the TODO list right now?" - "Add this paper to our bib file" (paste a DOI or paper title) - To switch to the project's Zotero group library, say: Use zotero_switch_library with library_id="<NUMBER>" and library_type="group" (Whoever manages the project's Zotero library will tell you the group ID.)

docs.title: Troubleshooting: "Rscript is not recognized" / R not installed
docs.text:
The step-5 verification fails for two different reasons that look the same:

  • R is installed but not on PATH (the default on Windows — the R installer does not add itself). Use the full path instead of Rscript:
"C:\Program Files\R\R-4.4.3\bin\Rscript.exe" code/00_setup.R

(Adjust the version number to whatever sits under C:\Program Files\R\.)

  • R is not installed at all. Install from https://cran.r-project.org/ — pick the latest 4.4.x release. You do NOT need RStudio for the setup check; plain R is enough. After installing, use the full path above.

The same logic applies to python: if the bare name fails, use the full path from the project CLAUDE.md (on Kai-team Windows machines that is the Anaconda install, e.g. C:\ProgramData\anaconda3\python.exe).

docs.title: Project-specific notes
docs.text: Anything project-specific (target journal, current revision status, naming conventions, co-author preferences) lives inside the project's own CLAUDE.md file, not here. The file in this repo is for the general per-project workflow that applies across all projects.

docs.title: A practice run (throwaway repo)
docs.text:
Why do this. The git collaboration loop — branch, edit, commit, push, pull-request, merge — is muscle memory once you've done it twice, and nerve-wracking until you have. This page is a safe, throwaway practice run on a scratch file so your first real edit isn't also your first time learning the steps. Nothing here touches the paper or anyone else's work. Do it once, on your own, before your first real task.

You can do every step by hand or by asking Claude — both columns are shown. Pick whichever you'll actually use day to day; trying both once is a good way to decide.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need a clone set up already (the setup walkthrough gets you there). Confirm you're in it: you should be inside clone_<XX>/, not at the shared container root. If unsure, run the clone check first.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
Step By hand Ask Claude 1. Make a practice branch git checkout -b <XX>/practice "Make a branch called <XX>/practice." 2. Create a scratch file create practice-<XX>.md, type a line "Create a scratch file practice-<XX>.md with a sentence in it." 3. See what changed git status then git diff "Show me what changed." 4. Commit it git add practice-<XX>.md then git commit -m "practice commit" "Commit just that file with the message 'practice commit'." 5. Push the branch git push -u origin <XX>/practice "Push my practice branch." 6. Open a pull request open the link GitHub prints, click Create pull request "Open a PR for my practice branch." 7. Merge it on GitHub, click Merge (anyone can — no lead) (do this one on GitHub yourself, to see it) 8. Bring main back home git fetch origin && git merge origin/main "Pull the merged main into my branch."

That's the entire real-work loop. Every actual task is just this with a meaningful file instead of a scratch one.

docs.title: What you just learned to feel
docs.text:
• Branches are cheap and safe. You made one, used it, merged it, and nothing else was affected. Real work is the same.
  • git add takes explicit paths. Step 4 names the file on purpose — the house rule is never git add -A / git add ., so you never sweep in something you didn't mean to.
  • Pushing ≠ merging. Step 5 shared your branch; step 7 put it into main. Two separate, deliberate actions.
  • Pulling main is a separate habit. Step 8 is the one people forget — your clone won't show others' merged work until you explicitly merge origin/main in.

docs.title: Clean up (optional)
docs.text: Delete the scratch file in a follow-up commit, or just leave it — it's harmless. If you want the branch gone after merging, GitHub offers a Delete branch button on the merged PR; locally, git checkout <XX>/<your-working-branch> (whatever branch you normally work on) and carry on.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Now do a real small thing: fix a typo, add a citation, regenerate a figure. The loop is identical. The handbook has the day-to-day detail; common issues covers anything that looks off.

docs.title: Git
docs.text: Read this once, before any setup guide, if you've never used git or GitHub. Nothing here requires installing anything; after it, the install guides read as steps instead of incantations. (New to the terminal or Claude Code? Each has its own page in this section.)

docs.title: The whole workflow in one paragraph
docs.text: Your project lives in a Dropbox folder, like always. Two things are added on top. First, git — a version system that lets you take numbered snapshots of your work ("commits") and keeps every snapshot forever, so paper_v7_final_FINAL.tex filename gymnastics disappear: there is ONE file, and the history lives behind it. Snapshots are shared through GitHub (a website that hosts the project's history), so co-authors exchange work as reviewed, deliberate packages instead of silently overwriting each other in Dropbox. You never need to master git — you need ~10 concepts and 5 habits (below), and an assistant like Claude Code can handle the actual syntax while you approve each step. It's a fast assistant, not autopilot.

docs.title: The concepts (each with the economist's translation)
docs.text: Term What it means for you repository ("repo") The project's shared folder plus its full edit history — a Dropbox folder that also remembers every draft ever made. clone Your personal, complete copy of a repository, kept in sync with the shared original on GitHub. Every project has exactly ONE repo — the project root, every clone_<XX>/ folder, and GitHub's copy are all clones of it. Nobody creates a "second repo" for a co-author; they get another clone. commit A numbered draft snapshot with a one-line note — paper_v7 without you managing the numbering. You can always return to any commit. push Upload your snapshots to GitHub so co-authors can get them. Saving alone shares nothing — this is the #1 surprise. pull Download co-authors' snapshots into your copy. Do it before you start working. branch A parallel working draft — like a "robustness-checks version" of a do-file — that cannot disturb the main version until it's reviewed. main The one version guaranteed to compile: the journal-submission copy. You never edit it directly. pull request (PR) Asking the team to referee your branch and fold it into main — peer review for code and text. merge The step that brings branches together: combines two branches' commits into one history. Automatic — unless both touched the same lines (next row). Merge combines text; it does not check conventions. The PR review is where conventions get checked. merge conflict Two people edited the same lines; git shows both versions and asks a human to choose. Annoying, never fatal. gitignored Files on a "never goes into git" list (.gitignore): data, PDFs, private notes. Git acts as if they don't exist, so they can't leak. terminal / CLI A window where you type commands instead of clicking. See docs/terminal-101.md — 10 minutes. PATH The list of folders your computer searches when you type a program's name. "X is not recognized" usually means: close and reopen the terminal, or the program isn't installed. markdown (.md) A plain-text file with light formatting. Open in any editor, or read it nicely rendered on github.com. Claude Code An AI assistant living in the terminal. It reads the project's rule file (CLAUDE.md) on every start and asks before doing anything risky. token The unit your Claude subscription meters — like mobile data. Pasting documented commands is nearly free; asking Claude to figure out a setup conversationally burns hours of it. Hence: copy-paste the documented blocks. Personal Access Token (PAT) A generated stand-in for your GitHub password. When git asks for a password and you paste it, the screen stays blank — that's normal; press Enter. MCP server A small bridge program that lets Claude Code talk to an outside service (e.g. Zotero). Install once, forget. Node.js / npm The runtime Claude Code is built on, and its installer. Install once in Step 1, never think about it again.

docs.title: The five habits (all you actually need)
docs.text:
1. Pull before you start. git pull — get the team's latest before editing. (One command, or ask Claude: "pull the latest".)
  2. Save ≠ Commit ≠ Push. Save (Ctrl-S) protects against a crash. Commit creates a snapshot. Push shares it. All three, in that order, make work safe AND shared.
  3. Branch before editing. Never work directly on main. Ask Claude: "make a branch for the robustness tables".
  4. Commit at every clean checkpoint, push at the end of every session. Your own branch — push freely; that's your backup.
  5. When anything feels wrong: stop, don't improvise — run git status, or ask Claude "what's the state here?", or email Kai with the exact message. Almost nothing here is unrecoverable if you stop and ask before improvising — improvised "fixes" (and force-pushes) are the only real danger.

docs.title: Why the team works this way (the 60-second logic)
docs.text: Dropbox alone can't say which version of the code produced Figure 3, or let two people edit the same file without silently overwriting each other. Git alone can't hold gigabytes of data or sync it instantly. So the system uses both, each for what it's good at: Dropbox carries the files (especially data — one canonical copy, never duplicated), GitHub carries the meaning (who changed what, what was reviewed, what is production). Every rule in the handbook follows from that split — the full reasoning, with diagrams, is in docs/concepts.md.

docs.title: Where to next
docs.text:
1. docs/terminal-101.md — if you've never typed a command (10 min).
  2. The README install guide — every step is copy-paste, with "you should see…" checks.
  3. docs/co-author-onboarding.md — if you only edit paper text.
  4. docs/co-author-handbook.md — the daily workflow, once installed.

docs.title: What goes where — the project structure
docs.text:
Why a fixed structure at all. When several people share a project, the single biggest source of friction is not knowing where things live — so figures get lost, two people invent two data/ folders, and "where's the latest draft?" becomes a daily question. A shared, predictable layout removes that friction.

This is a working solution, not the solution. The goal here is not a structure that is theoretically perfect for economists — it's one where several people stay coordinated with low friction and it works in practice. If your team prefers a different arrangement, fine; what matters is that everyone uses the same one and that it keeps you out of the failure modes in why collaboration is hard. The layout below is the one this kit is built around, and the tools assume it.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
project-root/                  (the Dropbox folder; in multi-clone, a container)
├── CLAUDE.md                  project conventions Claude Code reads on entry
├── README.md                  human-facing: what this project is
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                   ORIGINAL data — read-only, never edited
│   ├── processed/             analysis datasets, built from raw by code
│   └── documentation/         codebooks, data dictionaries (git-tracked)
├── code/                      00_setup · 01_cleaning · 02_analysis · 99_run_all
├── output/                    figures/ · tables/ · maps/  (generated by code)
├── paper/                     paper.tex · references.bib · dated PDFs · old/ · presentations/
├── literature/                reference PDFs — LOCAL ONLY (gitignored)
├── project_management/        TODO, notes, submission log
└── temp_claude/               scratch (gitignored)

(On multi-author projects each person works in a nested clone_<XX>/; data/ stays once at the container — see why collaboration is hard.)

The same, as a picture:

flowchart TD
    R["project-root/<br/>(Dropbox folder; a container in multi-clone)"]
    R --> D["data/"]
    D --> RAW["raw/ — read-only, never edited"]
    D --> PROC["processed/ — built from raw by code"]
    D --> DOC["documentation/ — codebooks (git-tracked)"]
    R --> C["code/ — 00_setup → 99_run_all"]
    R --> O["output/ — figures · tables · maps (generated)"]
    R --> P["paper/ — paper.tex · references.bib · PDFs"]
    R --> L["literature/ — PDFs (local only, gitignored)"]
    R --> PM["project_management/ — TODO · notes · log"]
    R --> T["temp_claude/ — scratch (gitignored)"]

docs.title: What belongs in each folder — and why
docs.text:
Folder What goes here Why data/raw/ The original data, exactly as obtained It's the one thing you can't regenerate. Read-only, so a script can never corrupt your ground truth. data/processed/ Analysis datasets built from raw by code Derived = reproducible; if it's lost, you rebuild it. Keeps raw pristine. data/documentation/ Codebooks, variable dictionaries Small text that benefits from version control, so it's git-tracked while the heavy data isn't. code/ Numbered scripts (00_setup→99_run_all) One ordered pipeline anyone can run top to bottom; 00_setup owns all paths so nothing is hard-coded. output/ Figures, tables, maps — generated Every exhibit is reproducible from code/; nothing here is hand-made and unexplained. paper/ paper.tex, references.bib, dated PDFs The manuscript and its bibliography in one place; old drafts in old/. literature/ Reference PDFs Copyrighted + large → kept local, never committed. project_management/ TODOs, notes, submission log The admin layer, separate from the scientific work, so it doesn't clutter code or paper. temp_claude/ Throwaway scratch A clearly-disposable place so scratch never pollutes the real folders.

The deeper rationale (the two-layer model, the canonical-file rule) is in the ideas behind it; the full machine-readable spec is the canonical structure reference.

docs.title: Turning a messy project into this
docs.text:
Most real projects don't start this clean. Here's the before→after — and the one rule that comes first.

flowchart LR
    subgraph BEFORE["A typical messy project"]
        direction TB
        b1["Paper final v3/"]
        b2["Data and stuff/"]
        b3["analysis_FINAL.do"]
        b4["refs.bib"]
        b5["figures everywhere"]
    end
    subgraph AFTER["After: the shared layout"]
        direction TB
        a1["paper/  (paper.tex, references.bib)"]
        a2["data/  (raw, processed, documentation)"]
        a3["code/  (00_setup … 99_run_all)"]
        a4["output/  (figures, tables)"]
    end
    BEFORE ==>|"BACK UP FIRST, then restructure"| AFTER

Back up before you restructure — always. Restructuring renames and moves files; a mistake mid-move can lose work. So first: commit everything to git on a clean branch, AND/OR copy the whole project folder once (e.g. my-project_backup_2026-06-15/). With a backup, every later step costs nothing if it goes wrong.

Where you run this — and the order. A messy existing project has no clones yet, so you do the restructuring in a Claude Code session opened at the project folder itself (the existing messy root), not in a clone_<XX>/. The sequence is:

  1. Open Claude Code at the project folder → back up → restructure.
  2. If it's a multi-author project, --migrate-to-multi-clone then turns that folder into the shared container and helps you create your own clone_<XX>/.
  3. From then on, you open sessions inside your clone_<XX>/ for daily work (see set up your working clone). So the one-time restructure happens at the root; everyday work happens in your clone.

Then, three ways to get from messy to clean — pick what you're comfortable with:

  • With Claude Code (recommended): run /refactor-structure. It first shows a read-only plan (what it would rename/move), you confirm each step, and only then does it act — it never deletes. For multi-author projects, /refactor-structure --migrate-to-multi-clone then sets up the leaderless container + clones.
  • By hand: make the folders above and move files into them following the "what belongs where" table; then git add the new paths.
  • Starting fresh (new project): run /bootstrap-project — it scaffolds the whole layout + a CLAUDE.md for you. (Or create the tree by hand.)

Whichever you choose, the destination is the same layout — so the next person who opens the project already knows where everything is.

docs.title: Common tasks, step by step
docs.text:
The INDEX tells you what each tool does; this page tells you which tools to chain for a real task, with prompts you can paste verbatim. Six recipes cover ~80% of team usage.

How to read a recipe: the goal → why this chain → the steps with exact prompts. Prompts in code blocks are pasteable as-is into a Claude Code session opened in the project folder (adjust names in <angle brackets>).

Drift guard: scripts/release_check.sh verifies every command and skill named on this page still exists. If you rename a tool, this page fails the check until updated.

docs.title: 1. Start a new project (day 1)
docs.text:
Why this order: the project scaffold must exist before the paper scaffold (the paper lands inside it), and the replication metadata is cheapest to set up while the project is still empty — retrofitting it later is the painful version.

  1. Open Claude Code in the new (or messy existing) project folder. 
    /bootstrap-project
    Interactive: asks project mode, collaborators, Zotero setup, code stack; scaffolds the canonical folders + CLAUDE.md + .gitignore.
  2. If the project will have a LaTeX paper in git: 
    Scaffold the paper skeleton with /bootstrap-paper — title "<working title>", authors <names>.
  3. Wire the replication package early: 
    Run init-replication to set up the replication metadata.

Result: canonical folders, CLAUDE.md, paper skeleton, replication metadata — every later recipe assumes this baseline exists.

docs.title: 2. Add a figure to the paper
docs.text:
Why this chain: work happens on a branch so main always compiles; the figure skill picks the right data source and styling; the explicit copy step is what moves a finished exhibit into the PR (nothing happens "automatically on merge"). Full git mechanics: handbook §2.6.

  1. Branch first (in your clone, multi-clone projects): 
    Make a branch for the new conflict-trends figure.
  2. Build the figure — pick by type:
  3. Real-world data (World Bank, UCDP, V-Dem, OWID…): 
    Plot battle-related deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa 1990-2024 from UCDP, OWID style, save as conflict_trends_v1.
    (fires real-data-figure)
  4. Mechanism diagram / DAG / game tree: ask for a TikZ diagram (fires tikz-figure)
  5. Coefficient/event-study plot from a saved fit: /coef-plot
  6. Method-breakdown simulation: ask to "simulate what happens when the instrument is weak" (fires simulation-figure)
  7. The script writes to output/_exploratory/<your-branch>/figures/. When final, promote it — copy to canonical output/figures/ and commit script + exhibit + paper reference together (handbook §2.6 step 6 has the exact commands).
  8. Before the PR, check exhibit provenance: 
    /audit-exhibits
  9. Push the branch, open the PR.

docs.title: 3. Build or refresh the regression tables
docs.text:
Why this chain: the fragment pattern (table numbers produced by code, table skeleton living in the paper) is the house style — it keeps the AEA replication mapping clean and stops hand-edited numbers from drifting from the code. The least discoverable high-value tool in the toolkit.

  1. For each table: 
    /build-fragment-table — outcomes: <y1, y2>, treatment: <D>, FE: <unit, time>, cluster: <unit>. Print to chat first.
    Emits BOTH the Stata esttab block and the matching LaTeX outline with correct column counts.
  2. Data-sources appendix table (reads the replication metadata from recipe 1): 
    /build-data-source-table
  3. Survey/analysis projects with the two-codebook split — refresh the derived codebook after the pipeline ran: 
    /sync-codebook

docs.title: 4. The pre-submission gauntlet
docs.text:
Why this order: cheap checks first. The light review takes a minute and catches contribution/identification problems that would make the 30-minute full review a waste; the mechanical audits run last because they check the final text against the final numbers.

  1. One-minute pre-screen: 
    /review-paper-light
    Fix anything major it flags before proceeding.
  2. The full 6-agent referee report: 
    /review-paper <target journal>
  3. References are real and well-formed: 
    Run bib-audit on paper/references.bib.
  4. Every number in the text matches the code outputs: 
    Run audit-reproducibility against the manuscript.
  5. JEL codes for the title page: 
    /suggest-jel

(After an R&R: respond-to-referees exists but is HALTED pending its first real-world test — see working/TODO.md.)

docs.title: 5. Add a citation
docs.text:
Why three paths: not everyone has Zotero, and nobody should be blocked on bibliography plumbing. Full workflow: docs/co-author-onboarding.md.

  • No Zotero (anyone): type \citep{authorYEARkeyword} in the .tex, never touch references.bib — the key surfaces as a "pending orphan" for someone with Zotero to source.
  • One-off pull from Zotero: 
    /add-cite-from-zotero <citekey or title fragment>
  • Full refresh (read-only against Zotero, anyone can run): 
    /sync-bib

docs.title: 6. Which writing tool, when
docs.text:
Why this matters: four tools legitimately claim "review my text" and they do different things. Pick by what you want back:

flowchart TD
    Q["I have text. What do I want back?"] --> P["New or rewritten PROSE<br/>in Kai's voice"]
    Q --> DIAG["A DIAGNOSIS of the<br/>writing quality"]
    Q --> ORCH["Many things at once<br/>across a chapter/paper"]
    Q --> FLAW["Someone to attack it<br/>before I ship"]
    P --> P2["kai-writing (auto)"]
    DIAG --> D2["scientific-writing-analysis (auto)"]
    ORCH --> O2["/academic"]
    FLAW --> F2["adversarial-review (auto)"]
You want… Use Paste Text PRODUCED or REVISED in Kai's voice (intro paragraph, abstract, referee response prose) kai-writing skill Draft the contribution paragraph in Kai's style: <bullet points> A DIAGNOSIS of the writing (Lebrun codebook: progression, clarity, reader energy) — no rewriting scientific-writing-analysis Run a Lebrun analysis on the introduction. A multi-agent ORCHESTRATION across a whole chapter/paper (review + polish + figures + bib in parallel) /academic /academic review chapter 3 Hostile flaw-finding before you ship anything adversarial-review skill Red-team this draft before I send it.

(An AI-voice audit skill, humanize, exists but is currently HALTED — see working/TODO.md.)

Grants: /review-grant reviews a finished proposal. A grant drafting skill is planned (TODO Sprint 3).

docs.title: Replication packages
docs.text: Also tool-agnostic. A replication package is the bundle of data, code, and instructions that lets someone else (a journal, a referee, future-you) reproduce every number, table, and figure in your paper from scratch. This page is what one is and what goes in it; the toolkit has helpers that assemble it, but the concept and the discipline are general.

docs.title: Why bother
docs.text:
• Journals increasingly require it. Most leading economics journals (the AEA journals, and a growing list of others) now ask for a replication package as a condition of publication, checked before the paper appears.
  • Reproducibility is the credibility floor. A result nobody else can reproduce is, to a sceptical reader, not yet a result. The package is the evidence that yours holds.
  • Future-you is the first beneficiary. When a revision lands eighteen months later, a clean package means you re-run, not reconstruct.

docs.title: The cost of leaving it to the end
docs.text:
Reproducibility is cheap if you build it in and brutal if you bolt it on:

  • It's slow to retrofit. Reconstructing months later which script made which table, which data version was used, and what manual edits crept in is days of detective work — often more than the original analysis took.
  • It's sometimes impossible. If raw data was overwritten, a figure was hand-tweaked and never coded, or a number came from an interactive session nobody saved, you simply can't regenerate it. The trail is gone.
  • It's embarrassing — and a credibility hit — if it doesn't reproduce. The worst time to discover your results don't rebuild is when a journal's replicator (or a referee) tries and fails. "We can't reproduce our own numbers" is a bad sentence to write, and an even worse one to have written about you.

The fix is not heroics at the end — it's the small disciplines below, kept from day one (they're the same ones in organizing a research project).

docs.title: What goes in one
docs.text:
A good package is essentially your project's reproducible core, packaged:

  • Data — the raw data, or, if it's proprietary/confidential, a precise data-availability statement: what the data are, where to get them, and any access terms. (Never ship data you're not licensed to redistribute.)
  • Code — the cleaning and analysis scripts, in runnable order, with one master script (99_run_all) that executes the whole pipeline end to end.
  • A README — what to install, in what order to run things, expected runtime, and a mapping from each exhibit in the paper to the script that produces it.
  • Documentation — codebooks / data dictionaries for the variables.
  • The outputs — the figures and tables, so a checker can diff what they regenerate against what's in the paper.

docs.title: How the folder structure makes it (almost) free
docs.text:
This is the payoff of organizing the project well from the start: if you've kept data/raw immutable, built data/processed from code, generated every exhibit into output/ from numbered scripts, and kept a 99_run_all, then the replication package is basically already assembled — it's your project minus the scratch and the literature PDFs, plus a README and a data-availability statement. Teams that bolt reproducibility on at the end spend days; teams that follow the structure spend an afternoon.

The discipline that makes it cheap: the same "raw is read-only, code makes everything, one canonical pipeline" rules from organizing a research project. The package isn't a separate effort — it's what a well-organized project already is.

If you use the toolkit, the helpers that assemble and check the package are init-replication (scaffold it), build-data-source-table (the data-sources appendix), and audit-reproducibility (a pre-submission check that every exhibit traces to code) — see what's inside. But the package is a general deliverable; you can assemble it by hand from the checklist above.

docs.title: Reviewing with adversarial agents
docs.text: Before you ship a paper, grant, figure, plan, or chunk of code, the toolkit can run it past agents whose job is to find what's wrong, not to tell you it's fine. Here's the pattern and how to run it.

docs.title: Why adversarial, and why separate agents
docs.text:
Ask the agent that wrote something to check its own work and it tends to agree with itself: it has committed to an approach and is poorly placed to see that approach's weakness. (You miss typos in your own drafts for the same reason.) A separate agent starts fresh and judges the work on its merits, which is why peer review catches more than self-review.

So the reviewers are two things at once. Adversarial: told to break the work, assuming it's flawed until shown otherwise. Independent: a fresh context, not the agent that produced it. Run several in parallel and the catch rate rises, since each finds flaws the others miss.

docs.title: How to fire it
docs.text:
You want to check… Use What it does Any artefact (figure, plan, design, code, draft) adversarial-review Spawns independent flaw-finders; returns a graded findings list (HALT / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW / NIT), not a thumbs-up A paper, full pre-submission referee report /review-paper A 6-agent panel for a named journal — contribution, identification, consistency, maths, tables, claims A paper, fast pre-screen first /review-paper-light A ~1-minute 2-agent check (contribution + identification) before you spend time on the full report A grant proposal /review-grant A 6-agent funder-panel review Changed code /code-review Reviews the diff for correctness and cleanups

You can also just describe it: "spawn two independent agents to find the weakest points in this, default to skeptical." That's how you check a plan before approving it (see Working with Claude Code).

docs.title: The heavyweight option: COARSE
docs.text: For a referee-grade review of a finished paper, the referee-report workflow runs COARSE under the hood — David van Dijcke's open-source multi-agent peer-review pipeline (coarse.ink). It simulates a real referee across many agents and returns a structured report. It's the most thorough option; the lighter skills above are for faster checks while you work.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text: Run it before anything leaves your hands: a draft to co-authors, a figure going into the paper, a plan before you execute it, code before a merge. It costs a few minutes and saves you from shipping the flaw. Adversarial review is the default here; a balanced "tell me what's good" review is the exception you ask for.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: → Working with Claude Code · Self-correcting figures & diagrams · How it works — skills, processes & gates

docs.title: Self-correcting figures & diagrams
docs.text: When an agent makes a figure, you shouldn't be the one who notices the legend covers a bar or the axis says "millions" when it means "thousands." The agent can see those things itself, if it's told to look. This page is about making "build it, check it, fix it, then show me" the default, so you stop spending time on mistakes the agent could have caught.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
A good figure process is a short loop, run before you ever see the result:

  1. Build the figure.
  2. Render it and actually look at it.
  3. Self-check for the obvious problems — a legend overlapping the data, unreadable or overlapping labels, a wrong unit, a mislabelled axis, a colour that disappears, a title that doesn't match the data.
  4. Fix what's wrong and repeat once or twice.
  5. Then show you the result.

What reaches you is a checked draft, not a raw first attempt. You still judge the substance — but you're not doing the agent's proofreading.

docs.title: How it's set up today (soft, but reliable)
docs.text: The figure skills already work this way: real-data-figure and the TikZ/diagram skill instruct exactly this build → check → fix loop when you invoke them. That makes it a soft rule — an instruction the model follows when the skill runs (see how it works for the soft-vs-hard distinction).

docs.title: Turn it on everywhere (one line in your global config)
docs.text:
The skills cover figures made through them. To make the self-check apply to any figure or diagram Claude builds for you — in any project, with or without a skill — add one instruction to your personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (the global file Claude Code reads in every session). Paste this under a heading there:

## Figures & diagrams
When you create or edit any figure or diagram, do not show me the first
attempt. Render it, look for obvious problems (legend/label overlap,
unreadable text, wrong units, mislabelled or missing axes, a title that
doesn't match the data), fix them, and iterate up to 3 times. Only then
show me the result, and tell me briefly what you checked and changed.

From then on, every figure request should get the loop, not just ones that go through a figure skill. It costs nothing and removes a whole category of back-and-forth.

docs.title: What's not yet automatic
docs.text: This is still a soft rule: Claude follows the instruction, but nothing forces the check to run. The hard version — a hook that fires automatically after any figure file is written, renders it, and reviews it without being asked — is on the roadmap. It needs care to work the same on Mac and Windows, so it's a deliberate, tested addition rather than something to rush into everyone's setup. Until then, the global rule above is the reliable way to get the behaviour everywhere.
