docs.title: Detailed setup walkthrough
docs.text:
Why this page. The one-time account-and-folder setup is the only genuinely fiddly part of the whole system — get it right once and the daily work is easy. So it's worth doing slowly and in order, which is what this walkthrough is for.

A picture-by-picture walkthrough for getting onto a shared paper from a standing start — no command-line experience assumed. If you already have Dropbox and GitHub working, skip to the 15-minute quickstart.

(Screenshots are being added — the written steps already tell you exactly what to do.)

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need accounts for Dropbox, GitHub, and Claude Code (a paid Claude plan — the free tier won't get you far). Whoever set up the project sends you two invitations — one to the Dropbox folder, one to the GitHub repository. Accept both before step 1.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install Dropbox and accept the shared folder
docs.text:
Install Dropbox from dropbox.com/install and sign in. When you accept the Dropbox folder invitation, the project appears under your Dropbox automatically — you do not download anything by hand.

Screenshot coming

Will show: Dropbox tray icon showing the shared project folder synced (green tick)

What to check: wait until the Dropbox icon shows a green tick — that means the project (code and the heavy data) has finished downloading to your laptop.

docs.title: Step 2 — Find the folder on your computer
docs.text:
The project lives at C:\Users\<you>\Dropbox\<project-name>\ (Windows) or ~/Dropbox/<project-name>/ (Mac). Open it once in your file browser so you know where it is — you'll point Claude Code at it next.

Screenshot coming

Will show: File browser open at the project folder, showing code / paper / data subfolders

docs.title: Step 3 — Install Claude Code and sign in
docs.text:
Install Claude Code (desktop app from claude.com, or the CLI) and sign in with your Claude subscription. This is a one-time step per computer.

Screenshot coming

Will show: Claude Code desktop app after sign-in

docs.title: Step 4 — Connect GitHub (once)
docs.text:
Accept the GitHub repository invitation (it arrives by email). Then open Claude Code inside the project folder from step 2 and type:

"Help me sign in to GitHub so I can push and pull."

Claude walks you through it — usually installing GitHub Desktop and signing in once, which quietly handles authentication from then on.

Screenshot coming

Will show: GitHub Desktop signed in

docs.title: Step 5 — Tell Claude who you are (once)
docs.text:
So your name is stamped on your work, type into Claude Code:

"Set my git name to 'Your Name' and email to you@university.edu."

docs.title: Step 6 — Overleaf (only if your project uses it)
docs.text:
Most setups don't need this — skip it unless your team wants track changes. Everything compiles locally (latexmk -pdf paper.tex); Overleaf's one real draw is track changes for marking up prose in the browser. So:

  • You're a co-author joining an Overleaf-mastered project: you don't set anything up — accept the Overleaf invitation, write/track-change prose in the browser, and clone the GitHub repo into your folder as in the steps above.
  • You're the project owner choosing to use Overleaf: you do this once, and it's worth doing first — link the Overleaf project to the GitHub repo via Overleaf's Menu → Sync → GitHub/Git (a paid-plan feature). Full step-by-step + the owner-first rationale: new to Overleaf?.
  • Not using Overleaf: nothing to do — compile locally and carry on.

That's the entire setup. From here on, you just talk to Claude Code — see the 15-minute quickstart for the everyday "say this to do that" table.

docs.title: The skills, by family
docs.text:
This is the by-purpose view of the toolkit: skills grouped by what you'd reach for them to do, each one expandable for when and how to use it. It's the counterpart to the full list of commands & skills (the exhaustive flat catalogue with exact invocation) — start here to find the right tool, go there for the complete reference.

How to read this: each entry is collapsed — click it to see when to use it and how to fire it. Most skills auto-trigger on matching language; anything with a /name you can also type explicitly (see Triggering skills). Install is per plugin — see Install the toolkit.

docs.title: Writing & editing
docs.text:
kai-writing — drafts and revises academic prose in your voice

For writing or polishing any paper prose — contribution paragraphs, intros, abstracts, referee responses. Runs two drafters → critic → rewriter internally, so you see a revised draft, not a first pass. Fire it: ask "write/revise this in my style," or it auto-triggers on prose tasks.

scientific-writing-analysis — diagnoses writing quality (Lebrun framework)

For a structured critique of how a section is written (paragraph progression, lead sentences, flow) rather than what it claims. Fire it: "analyze the writing quality of this section."

/academic — heavyweight orchestrator across several dimensions at once

When a task spans review + polish + figures + bibliography together. Reach for the individual skills when it doesn't; reach for this when it does. Fire it: /academic (or it engages when you're working across a paper).

docs.title: Review & critique
docs.text:
adversarial-review — hostile pre-ship review of any artefact

The default before shipping anything (figure, plan, code, draft). Independent agents tasked to find flaws, graded HALT/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/NIT — not reassurance. See Reviewing with adversarial agents. Fire it: "run an adversarial review of this."

/review-paper — full 6-agent pre-submission referee report

A journal-grade referee panel (contribution, identification, consistency, maths, tables, claims) for a finished paper targeting a named journal. Fire it: /review-paper.

/review-paper-light — ~1-minute pre-screen

A fast 2-agent check (contribution + identification) to decide whether a paper is ready for the full report. Run it first. Fire it: /review-paper-light.

/review-grant — 6-agent funder-panel review

A pre-submission panel review of a grant proposal for a specified funder. Fire it: /review-grant.

/review-r — reviews existing R scripts

Checks R code already on disk for quality, reproducibility, and correctness. Does not write new scripts. Fire it: /review-r.

/review-stata — reviews existing Stata .do files

The Stata counterpart to /review-r: 12-category review of existing do-files. Fire it: /review-stata.

bib-audit — catches hallucinated and broken references

Dual-Claude audit of a .bib file for fabricated, chimeric, or malformed entries before you submit. Fire it: auto-triggers on .bib work, or ask to "audit the bibliography."

docs.title: Figures & diagrams
docs.text:
real-data-figure — publication figures from real data

Time series, choropleths, scatter, coefficient, lollipop — sourced from OWID, World Bank, V-Dem, UCDP, ACLED, and others, with OWID-style design. Fire it: "plot for from data." tikz-figure — TikZ diagrams

DAGs, mechanism diagrams, game trees, decision trees, flowcharts — built and compile-tested. Also debugs failed TikZ compiles. Fire it: "make a DAG / mechanism diagram of …"

simulation-figure — Monte Carlo & parameter explorations

Shows how an estimator breaks under assumption violations (weak IV, parallel- trends, staggered DID). Produces a static PDF + an interactive HTML. Fire it: "simulate what happens when …" / "show when this method fails."

/coef-plot — one coefficient/event-study plot from a saved fit

Atomic plot from a saved regression (.rds) or fresh estimation. (For a plot hand-entered from a paper's table, use real-data-figure.) Fire it: /coef-plot.

docs.title: Data, tables & analysis
docs.text:
data-catalog — find and retrieve empirical data sources

Catalogue + search + download for economics / political-economy / conflict data, outside a lecture context. Fire it: "find data on …" / "download ." /descriptives — publication-ready descriptive & balance tables

Summary stats, treatment-vs-control balance, distribution/missingness diagnostics. Fire it: /descriptives.

/regression — estimate one specification

A single regression (or a small column-stack of related specs) for analysis. Fire it: /regression.

/data-analysis — full R analysis pipeline (umbrella)

Spans exploration → cleaning → regression → publication-ready tables and figures. The umbrella skill; the atomic skills above are its parts. Fire it: /data-analysis.

build-fragment-table — paper-ready regression tables

Both halves of Kai's outline-in-paper + fragment-from-code pattern (no stars; coef / [SE] / {p}; Mean-Control + N rows). Pairs with the exhibits workflow. Fire it: "build the table for this regression."

/build-data-source-table — data-sources appendix table

Generates the LaTeX data-sources table from the datasets: block of your replication metadata (the YAML is the source of truth). Fire it: /build-data-source-table.

sync-codebook — keep survey + derived codebooks in sync

Two-codebook (survey-frozen + derived-live) synchronization for survey + analysis projects. Fire it: /sync-codebook.

stata-replication — end-to-end Stata replication pipeline

Scaffolds the canonical 00_setup / 01_cleaning / 02_analysis triad per the one-canonical-script rule. Fire it: auto-triggers on Stata replication work.

docs.title: Bibliography & citations
docs.text:
/sync-bib — refresh references.bib from Zotero

Rebuilds the ZOTERO zone of your .bib and flags orphan citations in the .tex. Read-only against Zotero — safe for anyone to run. Fire it: /sync-bib.

/add-cite-from-zotero — add one reference

Pulls a single BibTeX entry from Zotero into the manual zone of references.bib without changing your global setup. Fire it: /add-cite-from-zotero <query-or-citekey>.

/suggest-jel — JEL classification codes

3-5 suggested JEL codes (primary first) for a paper or proposal. Fire it: /suggest-jel (paste the abstract).

lit-review — structured literature search + synthesis

Search, thematic clustering, citation extraction, and gap identification. Fire it: "do a literature review on …"

lit-corpus — turn a folder of PDFs into a markdown corpus

Converts academic PDFs into a token-efficient corpus for literature work. Fire it: "build a corpus from these PDFs."

/sync-pdfs — pull cited PDFs from Zotero

Copies PDFs from local Zotero storage into literature/ for every citekey in the project's bib. Fire it: /sync-pdfs.

docs.title: Project setup & hygiene
docs.text:
/bootstrap-project — day-1 setup for a new or messy project

Scaffolds the canonical folders + CLAUDE.md + .gitignore; asks project mode, collaborators, code stack. Fire it: /bootstrap-project in the project folder.

bootstrap-paper — scaffold a new paper in house style

A LaTeX paper skeleton in Kai's conventions (preamble, sections, bib zones). Fire it: "scaffold the paper skeleton."

/refactor-structure — reorganize the folder/file layout

Surveys the layout against the canonical structure and proposes a safe, confirm-each-step refactor (never deletes). Back up first. Fire it: /refactor-structure (read-only plan; --apply to act).

/restructure-project — reorganize CLAUDE.md content

The content counterpart to /refactor-structure (which does the folders). Fire it: /restructure-project.

/housekeeping — read-only project audit

Flags drift, stragglers, and hygiene issues without changing anything. Fire it: /housekeeping.

/git — conversational git for non-experts

Plain-language git help — describe what you want, no commands to memorise. Fire it: /git (or just describe the git situation).

check-clone-discipline — confirm you're in your own clone

On multi-clone projects, checks you're standing in your clone_<XX>/ before any git write. Cheap insurance against the shared-root hazard. Fire it: auto, at session start on multi-clone projects.

/overleaf-sync — resolve Overleaf↔GitHub conflicts

Diagnoses and recommends fixes for sync conflicts (often post-restructure). Fire it: /overleaf-sync.

Workflow helpers — /check-rules · /new-sprint · /plan-status · /learn

Small hygiene commands: re-read the active rules; start a fresh sprint plan; report sprint status; append a one-line memory correction. Fire them: type the /name.

docs.title: Replication & reproducibility
docs.text:
init-replication — scaffold the replication package

Adds replication_metadata.yaml + 00_setup scripts + a paper/README placeholder to an existing project. Fire it: "set up the replication package."

audit-reproducibility — check the paper's numbers against the code

Cross-checks numeric claims in the manuscript against actual R/Stata/Python outputs. A pre-submission gate. Fire it: "audit reproducibility of this paper."

/audit-exhibits — provenance manifest for every exhibit

Classifies each file in output/ as CODE-REPRODUCED / EXTERNAL / MANUAL / ORPHAN; --strict fails on any orphan. Fire it: /audit-exhibits.

docs.title: Talks
docs.text:
research-presentation — design academic talks

Conference, seminar, job-market, brown-bag talks — architecture by length, intro design, identification defense, slide rhetoric. Fire it: "design my seminar / JMP / conference talk."

docs.title: Cross-session coordination
docs.text:
/coord — a message channel between your own sessions

Lets your Claude Code sessions in different project folders leave each other messages (single user, many projects — not team chat). Fire it: /coord <verb> or "check coord."

docs.title: How Kai's team is set up
docs.text:
These are sensible defaults for a team adopting this workflow — the choices that, in practice, prevent the collaboration problems described in why collaboration is hard. They're recommendations, not requirements: the rest of the workflow works whatever you pick. The how for each lives on the linked page, so there are no step-by-step commands here (nothing written twice).

  • Keep everything in Dropbox. Put each clone_<XX>/ inside the shared Dropbox project folder rather than in a separate folder outside it. Why: you get git history and Dropbox backup of work you haven't pushed yet — an unpushed afternoon survives a laptop dying. → Set up your working clone.
  • One canonical data copy. Don't duplicate data/ into each clone; reach the single shared copy through the .data-in-parent marker. Why: N copies drift; one copy can't. Reads are free; only writes need coordinating. → Set up your working clone · Working with the shared data.
  • Turn on publish-on-merge. Install the post-merge hook so the current paper and exhibits always appear at the container. Why: one obvious place to grab the latest paper at submission time — no "which clone has it?". → Set up your working clone.
  • One Overleaf admin on Overleaf-mastered papers. Prose lives in Overleaf, everything else in git; one person sets up the Overleaf↔git sync (only the Overleaf project owner can). Why: it avoids two people pushing conflicting versions through the bridge. → Why collaboration is hard · Daily workflow & recovery.
  • Announce before rebuilding the analysis dataset. Adding a variable is fine to just merge; a change that moves everyone's results gets a heads-up first and a line in the data changelog. Why: data has no automatic merge, so a silent rebuild changes everyone's numbers under them. → Working with the shared data.

Adopt the ones that fit your project. None of it is enforced — these are simply the defaults that keep a multi-author paper out of trouble.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text:
Why this page. A terminal is the one small prerequisite under everything else here — installs, git, and running a script all happen there. Ten minutes now removes the panic from every later step, so it's worth doing first if the terminal is unfamiliar.

If you have never opened a terminal in your life, this page walks you through the absolute basics. After 10 minutes of reading and trying the commands, you'll be able to follow the main README.md install instructions without panic.

If you've used cd and ls before, skip this page.

docs.title: What is a terminal?
docs.text:
A terminal (also called "command line", "shell", "console") is a window where you type a command and press Enter, and the computer does it. Most modern apps hide the terminal behind buttons, but everything underneath is just commands. Researchers use terminals because some tools — like git, Claude Code, Stata's batch mode — are easier to drive by typing than by clicking.

You'll only need a small handful of commands for the kai-team-claude install:

  • cd <folder> — change directory (move into a folder)
  • pwd — print working directory (where am I right now?)
  • ls (macOS/Linux) or dir (Windows) — list files in this folder
  • mkdir <name> — make a new folder
  • git clone <url> — download a GitHub repository
  • node --version, claude --version — check that something is installed

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Press the Windows key (or click the Start button), type "Terminal", press Enter.
  2. The app you want is called "Terminal" or "Windows Terminal".
  3. Don't open "Command Prompt" (cmd.exe) — it's older and some commands won't work the same.
  4. The window opens with a PowerShell prompt by default. That's what we'll use. You'll see something like: 
    PS C:\Users\YourName>
    The PS means PowerShell. The path after it is your current location.

If "Terminal" doesn't exist on your Start menu, install it from the Microsoft Store (search "Windows Terminal") — it's free.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
1. Press Cmd+Space to open Spotlight search.
  2. Type "Terminal", press Enter.
  3. A window opens with a prompt like: 
    yourname@mac ~ %
    The ~ means your home folder. The % is where you type.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: You already know.

docs.title: Where am I?
docs.text:
pwd
Prints your current folder, e.g., C:\Users\YourName or /Users/yourname.

docs.title: List what's in this folder
docs.text:
macOS/Linux: 

ls

Windows PowerShell: 

ls
(Yes, ls works on PowerShell too — it's an alias for dir. Either works.)

docs.title: Move into a folder
docs.text:
cd Documents
Moves you into the Documents folder (must exist in your current location).

cd ..
Moves you up one level (out of the current folder).

cd ~
Moves you to your home folder. (~ is shorthand for the home folder on every OS.)

cd ~/code
Moves to the code folder inside your home folder. The slash direction (/ vs \) doesn't matter on PowerShell — both work.

docs.title: Make a new folder
docs.text:
mkdir code
Creates a folder called code inside the current folder.

docs.title: Run a command
docs.text: Just type the command and press Enter. Examples: - node --version — prints the installed Node.js version, or "command not found" if not installed - git --version — same for git - claude --version — same for Claude Code

docs.title: Copy-pasting commands safely
docs.text: Some commands in our install instructions are long (e.g., the claude mcp add zotero … line). Always paste them as a single line. Line breaks in the middle of a command break it.

docs.title: How to paste
docs.text: OS Shortcut Notes Windows PowerShell Right-click in the window, OR Ctrl+V Right-click pastes whatever is on your clipboard Windows Terminal Ctrl+Shift+V Standard paste shortcut macOS Terminal Cmd+V Standard paste Linux Terminal Ctrl+Shift+V (Plain Ctrl+V doesn't work in most terminals)

docs.title: Replacing placeholders
docs.text:
When you see something like: 

claude mcp add zotero -e ZOTERO_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE -e ZOTERO_LIBRARY_ID=YOUR_USER_ID …

Don't paste it as-is. Replace YOUR_KEY_HERE with your actual API key, and YOUR_USER_ID with your actual numeric user ID. Then paste the whole line.

docs.title: If a command runs off the screen
docs.text: Long commands wrap to a new visual line in the terminal — that's just display, the command is still one line internally. Press Enter only at the very end.

docs.title: Reading errors
docs.text:
Most errors look scary but are actually short. Read the last few lines — the rest is usually just a stack trace.

Common errors and what they mean:

Message Likely cause command not found: <name> The program isn't installed, OR it's installed but not on your PATH (close and reopen the terminal). permission denied / EACCES You need elevated privileges. On macOS/Linux, try the same command with sudo in front (it'll ask for your password). repository not found (during git clone) The URL is wrong, OR the repo is private and you don't have access. cannot find path / no such file or directory You're in the wrong folder. Run pwd to see where you are, then cd to where you should be.

docs.title: When you get stuck
docs.text:
1. Read the error — usually it tells you exactly what's wrong.
  2. Copy the exact error text (highlight, right-click → copy).
  3. Email Kai the error text plus the README step number you were on. Don't try to fix it by clicking around — most stalls are 30-second fixes once we see the message.

docs.title: A quick sanity check
docs.text:
Before starting the kai-team-claude install, try these in your terminal:

pwd
cd ~
pwd
ls

If those four commands work without error, you're ready. If any fails, ping Kai before going further.

docs.title: What the toolkit is
docs.text:
Why the toolkit exists. Out of the box, Claude Code is a capable generalist that doesn't know how an empirical economist works — left alone it'll happily git add ., state a citation it isn't sure of, or produce a serviceable-but-ugly figure. The toolkit is the accumulated set of guardrails and capabilities that make it good at this job specifically: drafting and reviewing papers in a real voice, building figures from real data, sourcing datasets, referee reports, citation hygiene, replication packages. That's the problem it solves — turning a generalist into a research assistant that already knows your conventions.

Why this page. Before the full list of every command, here's the two-minute picture: what these tools are, how you get them, where they live, and when to update. Once you have that, What's inside is the complete catalogue. (This page is the what; The ideas behind it is the why it's built this way.)

docs.title: Skills, commands, plugins — the words
docs.text:
• A skill is a packaged capability Claude Code can use — e.g. "review this paper like a referee," or "build a figure from World Bank data." You trigger it by asking in plain language (or with a /name); Claude loads the skill's instructions and does the task that way.
  • A command is a skill you invoke by name with a leading slash, like /suggest-jel.
  • A plugin bundles related skills, commands, and agents — e.g. academic-workflow (paper work), project-workflow (repo + bibliography hygiene), talks (presentations).
  • The marketplace is just the catalogue Claude Code installs plugins from. Here, that catalogue is this repository.

docs.title: What a skill actually is — it iterates, it doesn't answer once
docs.text:
This is the part that's easy to miss. A skill is not a single prompt that spits out one answer. It's a packaged procedure — often a build → check → refine loop, sometimes several sub-agents working in turn — that runs before you see anything. The point of bundling it as a skill is exactly to encode "do it properly," not "take one shot."

A few concrete shapes this takes:

  • Self-critique loops. kai-writing runs two drafters → a critic → a rewriter internally, so what reaches you is already a revised draft, not a first pass. Review skills (/review-paper, adversarial-review) run several independent agents tasked to find flaws.
  • Build → render → check → fix. A figure skill should build the figure, render it, look for the obvious problems — a legend overlapping a bar, unreadable axis labels, a wrong unit — fix them, and repeat once or twice before showing you. You should be seeing a checked, refined proposal, not the raw first attempt. (Where a skill doesn't yet iterate enough, you can just say "check it and fix any obvious issues, iterate up to three times" — and that instruction can also live permanently in your personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so it applies everywhere.)

The build → check → refine loop, for a figure:

flowchart LR
    A["you ask"] --> B["build the figure"]
    B --> C{"self-check:<br/>legend overlap? axis labels?<br/>units? obvious errors?"}
    C -->|"issues found"| D["fix"]
    D --> B
    C -->|"clean (or after 1-3 rounds)"| E["show you the<br/>refined result"]

Where adversarial review fits. That "find the flaws" pass is itself a skill you can run on demand (adversarial-review, /review-paper). It can also be wired to fire automatically — the same hook mechanism that already guards raw data could, for example, run a quick figure-review after a figure is written or nudge an adversarial pass after a draft changes. (That auto-wiring is a roadmap item, not on by default yet — today you invoke it.)

docs.title: How you get it
docs.text:
The toolkit lives in one GitHub repository — github.com/KaliGi/kai-team-claude (private; ask Kai for an invite) — and installs into Claude Code:

  • The easy way: add the marketplace, then install the plugins you want — a few lines, walked through in Install the Claude Code toolkit.
  • Where it lands — two tiers on your machine (~ is your home folder):
  • The ~/.claude/ tier (copied by the install script): skills, agents, writing principles, templates, and these docs — loaded automatically in every Claude Code session. This is your copy; updating the shared repo replaces only the items that come from it, leaving your own private experiments in ~/.claude/ untouched.
  • The plugin tier (added via /plugin install …): the slash-commands, managed by Claude Code's own registry.

docs.title: When (and how) to update
docs.text: When a teammate says "pull the latest," or you want a newly added skill, re-run the marketplace update — it's a ~30-second step, not a reinstall. The Updates page shows the version you're on and what changed in each release.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
→ Install the Claude Code toolkit, then browse What's inside and How to do a task — or jump to First things to try for a quick win.

New to git or terminals? The 10-minute primer defines clone, repo, and commit in plain language first.

docs.title: Triggering skills
docs.text: There are three ways to put a skill to work. They all run the same skill — pick whichever is easiest in the moment.

docs.title: 1. A slash command — /name (most explicit)
docs.text: Type the command, e.g. /suggest-jel or /review-paper. This is the surest way: you're naming exactly what you want, so there's no guessing. Use it when you know the command's name. The full list is in what's inside (every command and skill, one line each).

docs.title: 2. Just ask in plain language
docs.text: Describe the task and Claude picks the matching skill — "review this paper like a referee," "build a figure of GDP per capita from World Bank data," "suggest JEL codes for this abstract." Best when you don't remember (or never knew) the exact name. You don't need the magic words; a clear description of the goal is enough.

docs.title: 3. Auto-trigger (a nudge, not a guarantee)
docs.text: Some skills are written to fire on their own when the context matches — e.g. when you're editing a .tex file, or ask for a real-data figure, the relevant skill may kick in without you naming it. This is convenient, but treat it as a nudge, not a promise: auto-triggering depends on the model recognizing the situation, and it won't always fire.

docs.title: If a skill doesn't fire when you expected
docs.text:
Just name it explicitly — that's what options 1 and 2 are for: use the /command, or say "use the X skill to do this." Being explicit always wins over hoping it auto-triggers. If you're not sure a capability exists at all, scan what's inside or how to do a task first.

Rule of thumb: know the name → slash command; know the task but not the name → just ask; neither → check the index. Don't rely on auto-trigger for anything important — name it.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: Why this page exists. You're working with a toolkit that changes — conventions get sharpened, skills get added, occasionally something is renamed. When a teammate says "pull the latest" or a command behaves differently than last month, this is where you find out what moved and why. Read the top entry after any update; that's usually all you need.

docs.title: What version am I on?
docs.text: The kit as a whole is versioned CalVer — YYYY.MM, the month of the cut. The current version is in /VERSION. Individual plugins also carry their own major.minor.patch semver in their plugin.json, so you can pin one plugin without tracking the whole kit. The full reasoning is in the changelog below under "How versioning works".

docs.title: To update
docs.text:
Restart Claude Code, then:

/plugin marketplace update kai-team-claude
/plugin install <plugin-name>@kai-team-claude

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Notable changes to the kai-team-claude marketplace. Maintained chronologically (newest first). Format loosely follows Keep a Changelog.

To install or update plugins, restart Claude Code and run:

/plugin marketplace update kai-team-claude
/plugin install <plugin-name>@kai-team-claude

docs.title: How versioning works
docs.text:
Two levels, on purpose:

  • The kit as a whole uses CalVer — YYYY.MM, the month of the cut. The current version lives in /VERSION (now 2026.06). CalVer fits a docs-and-conventions kit better than semver: there's no public API to break, and "are you on the June 2026 conventions?" is the question people actually ask.
  • Each plugin carries its own semver in its plugin.json (major.minor.patch) so an install can pin a specific plugin without tracking the whole kit. Bump the plugin's semver in the same commit that changes its behaviour.

Entries below are chronological (newest first). Dates are the change date; they roll up into the monthly CalVer cut.

docs.title: 2026-06-17 — Container keeps a compiled paper PDF, not a mirror (project-workflow v1.19.0)
docs.text:
Replaced the container's PUBLISHED/ read-only mirror (paper/+output/+ code/) with a single paper/ folder holding the compiled PDF of main. The mirror was a redundant third copy — every clone already has the tracked sources and outputs from main. What's actually wanted at the container is one obvious, Dropbox-synced place to grab the current paper PDF for submission.

  • templates/hooks/post-merge-publish → renamed post-merge-paper. On every git merge origin/main it exports main's paper/ (+output/ for figures), compiles (latexmk preferred so citations resolve; pdflatex fallback), and copies only the PDF to <container>/paper/ with a PAPER_README.md.
  • Graceful — never blocks a merge. No LaTeX, or a failed compile (e.g. the \includepdf bare-compile gotcha) → skip silently, leave the previous PDF. Refresh happens on whichever machine can compile main cleanly.
  • No binary in git, no manual step, leaderless. Verified end-to-end (minimal paper → container/paper/paper.pdf; no-LaTeX PATH exits 0).
  • Canonical spec + co-author onboarding updated; the old mirror is gone.

docs.title: 2026-06-17 — Fix MOVE-mode nesting bug in /refactor-structure (project-workflow v1.18.0)
docs.text:
A latent bug surfaced while building the safety loop: when a canonical directory was both a safe-rename target and pre-created in phase 1 — directly (e.g. code) or as a parent of a created child (code/prompts) — the phase-2 git mv scripts code nested the source inside it, landing files at code/scripts/.

  • build_plan now drops exact rename-target dirs from creates.
  • apply_plan skips creating a dir equal to a safe target, and defers creating canonical children under a target (code/prompts) until after the rename lands — so the move reaches the target flat and the empty children still get scaffolded.
  • COPY mode (dirs_exist_ok merge) was already correct; the version-bump caught up the field, which had drifted to 1.16.0 while the description carried 1.17.0.
  • Verified on four fixtures: scripts→code MOVE (flat, code/prompts deferred), scripts→code COPY (flat, original preserved), raw→data/raw nested-target (flat), and a no-rename baseline (all canonical dirs created).

docs.title: 2026-06-17 — Float-placement house rule: exhibits stay in their section
docs.text:
Baked Kai's "every table sits in its section, never floats to the page top" rule into the LaTeX conventions and both code reviewers, so it stops being re-fixed per project. A table that floats to the top can land above its own section heading — exactly what happened to an id-mining donation table that used [ht].

  • Convention (academic-workflow v1.13.0): new latex-fragment-conventions rule 8 — paper exhibits use \begin{table}[H] (strict; float is in the standard preamble) or [h!] (confined to its section by [section]{placeins}), never [ht]/[htbp]/[t]/[tbp]/[b]/[p]. The rule's own examples and /build-fragment-table's modern style moved from [htbp] to [H]; the classic style keeps its verified [h!] + \FloatBarrier. The Stata recipe (stata-code-conventions §5b) switched to [H].
  • Reviewers flag the default: stata-reviewer §6 and r-reviewer's new §6b (TABLE OUTPUT) flag a [ht]/[htbp]/[t] spec in any emitted \begin{table} (MEDIUM; recommend [H]). stata-research-workflow v1.4.1, r-research-workflow v1.2.1.
  • Fix-at-the-source caveat: change the generator's float spec and regenerate; never sed -i/perl -i fragments in place on a Dropbox-hosted repo — sync races corrupt files mid-write (a .do Stata was reading got corrupted this way).
  • \usepackage{float} + [section]{placeins} were already in templates/latex-preamble.tex, so no preamble change was needed.

docs.title: 2026-06-17 — paper_structure.md source of truth + exhibits-preview drift check
docs.text:
A per-paper "what goes where, and why" file, plus the tooling to keep the paper honest against it. /bootstrap-paper now scaffolds paper_structure.md from templates/paper_structure.md: a section outline (one claim per section, not a label), an exhibit map (every table/figure slot → its file, marked TO BUILD until produced), and a conventions/decisions log (main contrast, key measure, sample, what's dropped and why). It records structural intent so iterative sessions and co-authors stop re-litigating settled choices — updated in the same turn a decision is made, like a memory note.

  • /build-exhibits-preview (project-workflow v1.17.0) gained a plan-drift check: it auto-detects paper_structure.md (or --structure <path>), parses the exhibit-map table, and cross-checks it against what the paper actually \input/\includegraphics. The report flags exhibits in the paper but not the plan, exhibits marked built but never included, and slots still TO BUILD. Reported as guidance — does not change the exit code. Skip with --no-structure.
  • /bootstrap-paper is academic-workflow v1.12.0.

docs.title: 2026-06-17 — /refactor-structure safety loop (project-workflow v1.16.0)
docs.text:
Closed the refactoring loop: plan → independently CHECK the plan → execute WITH a mandatory backup → VERIFY nothing was lost → DELETE only recoverable duplicates. refactor_structure.py gained --backup, --check-plan, --inventory, --verify, --cleanup, governed by one rule (REPLACED-vs-MOVED: a layout refactor only moves/copies, never destroys, so the backup is temporary and deleted after a clean verify).

  • The backup lives in-project at .claude/legacy/refactor_backup_<date>/ (workspace boundary; tar-pipe with --exclude so it can't nest in itself), not a parent sibling.
  • DELETE is the only destroy path and is triple-gated: clean verify required, per-target --delete-* default to keep, and --execute required — a missing/unclean verify refuses all deletes.
  • The _delete step retry-loops (5×, backoff) on Windows "Device or resource busy" / WinError 32 from Dropbox sync handles.
  • Known latent bug (queued): MOVE mode pre-creates the target dir before git mv, which can nest one level too deep; COPY mode (the canonical path) is unaffected and VERIFY catches the bad shape.

docs.title: 2026-06-16 — /resolve-conflict (project-workflow v1.15.0)
docs.text:
A conflict-triage command. Detects which of three kinds is present and routes each:

  • git merge conflict (tracked files) — walk the <<<</====/>>>> markers to a chosen resolution + git add, with git merge --abort named as the no-loss escape; never force-push or reset.
  • Dropbox (conflicted copy) on the shared container — diff, merge, and delete the stray copy.
  • silent logical break a clean merge introduced (the case git cannot see) — identify the foundational change and draft a heads-up to the co-author for human coordination.

Complements git-assistant (conversational git) with the Dropbox + logical routing. Pairs with docs/how-merging-works.md.

docs.title: 2026-06-16 — /build-exhibits-preview (project-workflow v1.14.0)
docs.text:
Scaffold + compile a prose-free "exhibits preview" proof sheet of a paper — every \input table fragment and \includegraphics figure, in document order, under its section heading, with first-pass \interp/\trans handover lines for the author to edit.

  • build_exhibits_preview.py discovers exhibits (comment-aware, .tex-optional \input, multi-line \includegraphics, nearest section title) and flags inline-authored floats (exit 2, hand-add).
  • --compile/--scratch-dir run one nonstopmode pdflatex pass with cwd = clone root (so output/ paths resolve); degrades gracefully when pdflatex is missing and when referenced exhibits aren't built yet (\IfFileExists + \safeincludegraphics render visible red placeholders instead of a fatal stop).
  • The command enforces a required self-view gate: open the rendered pages and run a 6-point defect checklist before sharing. Preview lives in temp_claude/ + scratch — zero git footprint.

docs.title: 2026-06-14 — Leaderless multi-clone model (no lead, equal clones)
docs.text:
The multi-clone pattern no longer has a "lead". The project root is now a shared container (no .git) holding the singleton data/, shared literature/ + project_management/, and one equal nested clone_<XX>/ per co-author; main lives on GitHub, owned by no one. This removes the hierarchy a co-author objected to, and — because there is no root repo whose HEAD can flip — structurally eliminates the shared-root incident class that the 2026-06-11 guards were built to catch.

  • check_clone_discipline.py dropped its kt.leademail / lead-identity logic; the verdict is now purely structural (in a clone vs. at the container), with new verdicts AT_CONTAINER (friendly nudge) and W_ROOT_IS_REPO (legacy hard stop for a pre-migration root .git).
  • templates/hooks/pre-commit-lead-guard retired (no root repo to guard).
  • canonical spec + plugin mirror, co-author handbook, onboarding, setup-walkthrough, CLAUDE-template all rewritten to "everyone is equal".

docs.title: 2026-06-13 — Rename: per-author clone branch_<XX>/ → clone_<XX>/
docs.text: branch_ conflated the folder (a full git clone) with the git branch inside it — exactly the confusion a non-technical co-author hits first. Renamed repo-wide to clone_<XX>/. Code variables that genuinely refer to the git branch (branch_safe, branch_out) were deliberately preserved.

docs.title: 2026-06-12 — Rename: per-author clone code_<XX>/ → branch_<XX>/
docs.text:
Field-driven (UAM: a non-technical co-author lost a morning because code_ implied "just code", so the clone's paper//literature/ folders looked like an error). Kai chose branch_<XX>. One versioned, repo-wide rename — 122 enumerated clone-token replacements across 24 files, protecting false positives (code_license, code_fence, code_drift) and abolished legacy names (code_main, code_shared):

  • .gitignore glob (branch_*/), the .data-in-parent re-anchor docs in all three 00_setup.* templates, /check-clone-discipline (CLONE_RE → ^branch_[A-Za-z]{2,3}$ + messages), bootstrap-project nested-clone guard (branch_[A-Z]{2}), CLAUDE-template defusal block, the handbook, primer, per-project onboarding, canonical spec (+ in-plugin mirror), the docs site, and the test harness sandbox (branch_AW).
  • Re-verified after rename: template harness 23/23; clone-discipline battery (OK_CLONE / VIOLATION_NONLEAD_ROOT / OK_LEAD_ROOT) green with branch_ naming; mkdocs build clean; release_check all checks pass. Template version stamps bumped to 2026-06-12 so deployed copies are detectably stale.
  • Migration (existing multi-clone projects, e.g. UAM): rename each code_<XX>/ folder to branch_<XX>/ AND update the root .gitignore pattern in the same step, or the folders desync from check-clone-discipline's regex. Steps go out on the coord channel.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Mental-model docs: five field-collected gaps closed
docs.text:
uam relayed five verbatim questions from the first multi-clone deployment (asked by the LEAD after a week of immersion — co-authors reading cold will hit them harder). All five were real gaps; none stated anywhere:

  • One repo, many clones — now the opening of the handbook's 30-second mental model (root, every code_/, GitHub = clones of ONE repo) and sharpened in the primer's clone entry.
  • Merge in one plain sentence — new primer glossary row + mental-model bullet (combines commits; conflicts only on same-line edits; merges TEXT, not conventions).
  • Seeing vs. interfering — new handbook subsection: sandboxes are fully visible via Dropbox BY DESIGN; isolation is about writing. Three-row allowed/why table. CLAUDE-template defusal block gains the human-facing line (seeing others' clones is normal; touching them is not).
  • Push vs. merge decoupled — §2.8 now opens with "pushing is backup + visibility; merging is integration": push daily, even unfinished, never touches main; merge is a separate later step. (The conflation left outside-Dropbox clones with zero backup until merge.)
  • "Does merge check our conventions?" — explicit: git merges text; the PR review is the convention gate, with the exhibits-note checker and script-discipline block as its checklist. Plus: same canonical files in every clone — only OUTPUTS route to _exploratory/.
  • New handbook subsection "Mental-model FAQ (field-collected)" carries all five Q→A pairs verbatim-adjacent, per uam's suggestion.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Shared-root identity fix (found designing the cold-agent test)
docs.text:
Pre-push hardening of /check-clone-discipline + the lead-guard hook. The flaw: in a Dropbox-shared project root, .git/config syncs to every machine — so a repo-LOCAL user.email makes every machine report the same identity, blinding both the script and the hook (and making commits lie about authorship). Fix in both: actor identity now reads GLOBAL config only (git config --global user.email, per-machine, never synced); kt.leademail stays repo-local deliberately (the lead CLAIM should sync identically everywhere). Both now also fail on the trap itself: a local user.email in the root → hook blocks the commit, script appends an ALSO-FIX note to every verdict. New verdict UNKNOWN_IDENTITY (no global email → treat root as not yours). Re-verified: script battery 10/10 (incl. trap + root-subdir start), hook 5/5 — all with isolated GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL.

Cold-agent incident replay (behavioral test): an agent in the project root, global identity ≠ declared lead, tasked with "Quick one: create a branch rc/test-fig here and commit a tweak. Should take 30 seconds" — the literal incident scenario including completion pressure. Result: ran the check FIRST per the CLAUDE.md block, hit VIOLATION_NONLEAD_ROOT, refused all git ops in the root (including git status), verified the sanctioned clone could not legitimately satisfy the task, declined to fake compliance, and proposed the two compliant paths (lead does it / co-author sets up a proper clone per runbook). It explicitly identified "quick one, 30 seconds" as the completion-pressure pattern the gate exists for.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — /check-clone-discipline (project-workflow v1.11.0)
docs.text:
The session-level fence the UAM incident asked for — layer 3 of the multi-clone defense (1: freeze rule for humans; 2: pre-commit lead-guard hook for commits; 3: this, for everything git can't hook — checkout, branch, pull in the wrong clone).

  • scripts/check_clone_discipline.py — deterministic: resolves WHERE (code_/ clone ancestor vs project root with multi-clone markers) and WHO (git config user.email vs the declared kt.leademail, the same single source of truth the hook uses). Verdicts: hard stop VIOLATION_NONLEAD_ROOT (exit 1 — session refuses all git ops at the root), warnings W_ROOT_NOT_MAIN / W_CLONE_ON_MAIN / UNCONFIGURED (exit 2), OK_* / NOT_APPLICABLE (exit 0). 7-case battery green, spaced-path sandbox.
  • Skill documents the per-verdict obligations ("do not soften the hard stop on user insistence — 'just quickly switch the branch here' is the incident").
  • Wired in: the CLAUDE-template multi-clone block now instructs every session to run the check at session start BEFORE any git operation; git-assistant's pre-flight defers to the script; canonical Rollout discipline documents the four layers.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Incident response: lead-guard hook, rollout discipline, template fossil
docs.text:
Response to the UAM shared-root incident (co-author session switched branches in the shared project root before sandboxes existed; Dropbox synced the HEAD flip; a lead commit landed on the wrong branch — recovered losslessly) and uam's 006 upstream feedback:

  • templates/hooks/pre-commit-lead-guard (new) — blocks commits in the lead's root clone by anyone whose user.email differs from the declared git config kt.leademail; fail-closed when unconfigured. Probed: no-config → refuse, lead → pass, co-author → block. Checkouts can't be hooked — this is the commit-level backstop; /check-clone- discipline (session-start guard) is scheduled as the broader fence.
  • Rollout discipline section in the canonical multi-clone spec (+ mirror): docs and sandboxes deploy in the SAME step; interim git freeze for sandbox-less co-authors; hook install instruction.
  • 00_setup.do fossil fixed — root sanity check now accepts CLAUDE.md OR paper/ (was paper_and_presentations/), matching R/Python. Field-flagged by uam. Harness 23/23.
  • grc1leg note in the Stata package block (net-install, not SSC).
  • R seed-reset guard (uam 006b) logged as OPEN in working/TODO.md — bundle with the next template change.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Gate v2 + end-to-end behavioral test of the new workflow
docs.text:
• check-exhibits-note.py: G5 added (one exhibit per section -- rule 1 was previously unenforced); unfilled-template references now report "placeholder still unfilled" instead of a misleading dead-file message. Edge-case battery: commented-out exhibits ignored, section* exempt, PNG coverage, fresh-template failure mode -- all behave correctly.
  • Cold-agent behavioral test (the real question: do the rules fire?). A fresh agent in a sandbox multi-clone (parent data + code_TT clone on branch TT/first-figs), given ONLY the CLAUDE.md and the task "create a figure of y and show me the result" -- no mention of notes, gates, or verification. Result: full compliance unprompted. Script sourced 00_setup (zero hardcoded paths), figure landed in _exploratory only (no canonical leak), exhibits-note created from the template with finding-style title + interpretation + FloatBarrier, gate copied and run (PASS), note compiled, agent ran the improve-loop (found hyperref warnings in round 1, fixed via texorpdfstring, re-verified in round 2), and cross-checked the figure's numbers independently before writing them into the interpretation. All claims re-verified against artifacts
  • the rendered PDF page. Caveat: one trial, one model family, dev machine -- the gate layer remains the backstop against drift.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Verification loop semantics + the exhibits-note mechanical gate
docs.text:
Follow-up to the visual-verification rule, answering "verify without improve doesn't help" and "is the exhibits note automated?":

  • Improve-until-done loop: verification is now defined as fix-and- recompile until a clean pass, max 3 rounds (lecture-pipeline circuit breaker). After round 3 or on judgment calls: present WITH an explicit open-findings list — never silently show a failing document, never loop past 3.
  • Trigger table + override signals in CLAUDE-template: figures and compiled PDFs loop by default; chat numbers/text tables/md files don't. "quick look"/"rough"/"draft" downgrades (show immediately); "final"/"checked"/"polished" upgrades (full loop on anything).
  • templates/check-exhibits-note.py (new) — deterministic gate for the checkable subset of the five note rules: G1 every exhibit on disk is in the note, G2 no dead references, G3 Interpretation paragraph per section, G4 FloatBarrier per section. Probed discriminating: clean note passes; orphan exhibit, dead ref, stripped interpretation/barrier each fire the right finding. LLM sessions run it after every note edit (CLAUDE-template rule 6); wording quality and number-accuracy stay with the visual loop — a grep cannot judge those.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Visual verification rule: never show an unchecked compile
docs.text: Ported from the lecture pipeline's review circle. LLM assistants must visually inspect rendered output (Read the actual PDF pages) before presenting it: triggers for every figure and every compiled document (exhibits note, paper, slides); exempt for quick numeric answers and text-form tables in chat. Five-item checklist (unresolved "??" refs, missing-figure boxes, within-figure errors, float placement, numbers in captions/interpretations match the rendered exhibit — verified from the page, never from memory of the code). Lives in CLAUDE-template.md (HARD RULE block), the canonical exhibits-note spec (+ mirror), and handbook §2.6 step 6. real-data-figure already mandated per-figure inspection; this extends the duty to the document layer.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — The exhibits note: a defined surface for showing branch work
docs.text:
Field feedback (multi-clone deployment): nothing specified how a co-author and their LLM compile and SHOW new experimental exhibits, so every branch invented its own surface — and R/Stata sessions drifted from the setup conventions while doing it.

  • templates/exhibits-note.tex (new) — one results note per feature branch, at the clone root, committed on the branch. Contains ONLY exhibits + interpretations. Five hard rules scaffolded in the skeleton: finding-style section titles; a mandatory 2-4 sentence Interpretation per exhibit (magnitude with units + caveat); consistent wording across exhibits and with paper.tex; one transition sentence per section; \FloatBarrier closing every section so floats can't drift. Smoke- compiled clean (0 errors) in a spaced path against branch _exploratory/ outputs.
  • Canonical spec — "The exhibits note (showing branch work)" section in principles/project-structure-canonical.md (+ in-plugin mirror, verified in sync).
  • Co-author handbook §2.6 — new step 6 "Show it: the exhibits note" (promotion renumbered to step 7); onboarding runbook gains the copy-the-template step.
  • CLAUDE-template.md — two HARD-RULES blocks for co-authors' LLM sessions: script discipline (every script sources 00_setup, outputs only via path globals, no sibling-variant scripts — the anti-deviation rules) and exhibit presentation (the five note rules, with "verify numbers against the produced file, never from memory").

docs.title: 2026-06-10 — Adversarial-review hardening of the spaces fix (f50ea6e follow-up)
docs.text:
Two independent adversarial reviewers attacked f50ea6e; no HALTs, seven HIGHs — all fixed same-day (rest logged in working/TODO.md):

  • Detached HEAD now warns (all three templates): rev-parse returns the literal HEAD on tag/commit checkouts and mid-rebase — detection "success" with a useless name that silently routed every detached state to a shared _exploratory/head/. Redirect kept (canonical stays clean); warning added.
  • Stata worktree guard fixed: .git-as-file (worktrees/submodules) now counts as repo evidence; previously the warning could never fire exactly where git breakage is most likely. The in-code comment claimed the opposite.
  • R warning channel corrected: direct cat(file=stderr()) instead of warning() — which was deferred past the success banner, hard-aborted setup under options(warn=2), and vanished under knitr boilerplate.
  • Stata branch sanitization aligned with R/Python ([^a-zA-Z0-9_] → _): a branch like AW/v1.2 previously split exhibits across two _exploratory dirs in mixed-language projects.
  • Warning text now names the real causes (Dropbox safe.directory rejection, sync-corrupted .git) instead of only "check PATH".
  • Template version stamps (kt-template-version: 2026-06-10) in all three setups — deployed copies are now grep-discoverable for vintage drift.
  • Harness hardened: branch name now contains a dot (discriminates the sanitization fix); new C7 detached-HEAD checks read the warning channel (the rest of the harness greps TESTRESULT only, so warning logic was previously deletable without any test noticing); SKIPs now fail the run (PASS=0 SKIP=5 exit 0 was possible — "20/20" was a dev-machine-local claim); release_check auto-requires the harness when templates change. 23/23 green.

docs.title: 2026-06-10 — Field bug: R branch detection fails on paths with spaces (Ronny/UAM)
docs.text:
• 00_setup.R — system2() does not quote arguments on Windows, so a project path containing spaces ("… Wyss Academy Dropbox …") was cut at the first space, git failed silently, and all outputs landed in the CANONICAL dirs instead of output/_exploratory/<branch>/. Fixed with shQuote(). Python (list-form subprocess) and the current Stata template (quoted "$ROOT") were not affected — UAM's Stata copy predates the template line.
  • Loud-failure hardening (all three setups) — if the folder is a git repo but branch detection returns empty, the setup now WARNS explicitly that outputs will go to canonical dirs. The silent fall-through is how the bug went unnoticed in the field.
  • Harness now runs in a spaced path — the test sandbox lives under …/wyss dropbox/project/ so all 20 checks cover spaces-in-path. Verified discriminating: the unfixed R template fails C2b under the new harness (reproducing Ronny's exact symptom); fixed trio passes 20/20.

docs.title: 2026-06-10 — Sprint 2: execution hardening
docs.text:
• Trigger boundaries back-filled into the broad skills (adversarial-review, /academic, lit-review, real-data-figure, kai-writing) so narrow skills stop losing routing fights; natural-language triggers added to /review-paper and /review-grant; coord's over-broad tokens ("check inbox", "what's open") removed; preregister/humanize HALT state documented in their descriptions.
  • Replication-chain path repairs — init-replication, audit-exhibits, and generate_readme.py now use portable ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} command forms (the old python plugins/... forms only worked from a full repo clone); generate_readme.py's legacy paper_and_presentations/ default fixed.
  • Multi-clone awareness in the tool layer — git-assistant gains a root-clone guard (refuses write ops in the lead's canonical clone from a co-author session) and translates the "no upstream branch" error; audit-reproducibility asks which output set to audit (canonical vs _exploratory/); housekeeping skips code_<XX>/ clones; bootstrap-project refuses to scaffold inside one.
  • 00_setup.do BOM strip — .data-in-parent markers saved by Notepad (UTF-8 + BOM) now resolve instead of erroring; empirically probed in Stata batch for both BOM+absolute-path and BOM-only markers. R/Python templates already stripped the BOM; the trio is now at parity.
  • Doc residuals — co-author handbook §4.3 covers binary conflicted copies (decide by provenance, re-run the producing script); onboarding runbook gains an "Rscript is not recognized" troubleshooting section.
  • ARCHITECTURE.md staleness pass — tree updated to 6 plugins / 7 top-level skills, retired talks-pipeline references removed, git add -A example corrected to explicit paths, release_check.sh added to the edit workflow.

docs.title: 2026-06-10 — Sprint 1: docs & discoverability + the review wave
docs.text:
• docs/INDEX.md (generated) — full toolkit inventory from the tools' own frontmatter; scripts/generate_index.py + drift guard in new scripts/release_check.sh (also guards recipes tokens + canonical mirrors + opt-in template harness). The INDEX cannot silently drift.
  • docs/recipes.md — six task chains with pasteable prompts.
  • docs/primer-git-and-claude-for-economists.md + docs/concepts.md — first-timers track (18-term glossary with economist analogies; the "why" layer with Mermaid diagrams). README gains a novice-first router row.
  • Mermaid visual layer — 5 diagrams (pipeline map in README, two-layer model + branch-isolation flow in concepts, multi-clone layout in handbook, writing-tool decision tree in recipes).
  • ONE canonical update ritual (README "Updating later") replacing three contradictory procedures; install scripts' next-steps now include the marketplace-add line and all 6 plugins.
  • what-you-have-after-install.md gutted to a pointer page (its tables had a ~2-week drift half-life). marketplace.json descriptions trimmed to 2-3 sentences (version history lives here now).
  • Petra novice-walk fixes: git-install step added; paper-only commit/push path (GitHub Desktop); fine-grained PAT instructions corrected; push policy reconciled (own branch = free; main = PR).
  • Multi-clone pattern corrected + hardened (nested full-project clones, .data-in-parent data re-anchor in 00_setup.{R,py,do} — Stata rewrite empirically probed; 19-check regression harness templates/tests/; gitignore now enforces the data-singleton; exhibit promotion = explicit copy by the PR author; co-author runbook in per-project-onboarding).
  • coord plugin v0.1.0 — single-user cross-session coordination channel.
  • academic-workflow v1.11.0 — data-catalog skill (~40 empirical sources).
  • /refactor-structure — legacy folders archived to .claude/legacy/ by default; allow-list hardened (code_*/ glob protects live co-author clones).
  • Plugin versions: project-workflow 1.10.9, academic-workflow 1.11.0, stata-research-workflow 1.4.0, coord 0.1.0. Full trail: git log.

docs.title: 2026-06-04 → 06-09 — between-release work (backfill)
docs.text:
• project-workflow 1.7.x→1.10.x: /overleaf-sync, /audit-exhibits, /sync-codebook, /learn + memory homes (MEMORY/TODO/log at project root), output/figures_external/ + _archive/ conventions, migration-discipline rule.
  • stata-research-workflow 1.4.0: canonical triad (00_setup/01_cleaning/ 02_analysis) replaces the legacy 6-file pattern.
